example_sentence: Chào, lâu quá hông gặp!
example_translation: Hi, long time no see!
notes: Use as a casual, everyday greeting—friendly and informal. In Southern Vietnam people often use a shorter form instead of the more formal greeting.

example_sentence: Xin chào anh, dạ em giới thiệu chút xíu nha.
example_translation: Hello sir, I'd like to introduce myself briefly.
notes: Use in more polite situations (shops, offices); in the South it’s still used but sounds less warm and casual than "Chào".

example_sentence: Chào anh, anh khỏe hông?
example_translation: Hi bro, are you well?
notes: Use to greet a man who is slightly older or of higher status (but not much older); it conveys a respectful yet familiar tone and is common in Southern speech.

example_sentence: Chào chị, lâu rồi hông gặp chị luôn đó.
example_translation: Hi sis, haven't seen you in a while.
notes: Use when greeting a woman who is older than you or the same age but with whom you’re familiar; it’s a polite, casual “hi.” Very common in urban Southern Vietnam.

example_sentence: Chào em, hôm nay em sao rồi?
example_translation: Hi, how are you today?
notes: Use to greet someone younger or a subordinate; it’s friendly yet polite and fits casual to semi‑formal Southern Vietnamese.

example_sentence: Dạ, chào anh. Em có việc này muốn hỏi.
example_translation: Yes/hello sir. I have something to ask.
notes: A polite way to say “yes” or acknowledge someone—use it with elders or in formal situations; in the South people use “dạ” more often than “vâng.”

example_sentence: Ê, có khỏe hông mấy bữa ni?
example_translation: Hey, are you well these days?
notes: A friendly, very casual Southern way to ask "Are you well?" — the Southern pronunciation replaces "không" with "hông," so use it with friends and family and avoid formal situations.

example_sentence: Khỏe, cảm ơn anh. Còn anh sao?
example_translation: I'm fine, thanks. And you?
notes: A common, casual reply when someone asks how you are; you can add a polite particle (used to show respect) to make it more formal.

example_sentence: Lâu quá hông gặp, mừng quá thấy lại mấy đứa nè!
example_translation: Long time no see, so happy to see you guys again!
notes: Use this casual phrase when meeting someone you haven't seen for a long time. In the South people often add an informal question-tag (like "right?/no?") in spoken, friendly contexts, so avoid it in formal situations.

english: See you again / See you later
example_sentence: Hẹn gặp lại nha, mai mình uống cà phê tiếp.
example_translation: See you later, we'll grab coffee tomorrow.
notes: A casual, friendly farewell common in Southern Vietnamese—adding "nha" softens it and sounds warm; use with friends, family, or informal acquaintances, not in formal situations.

example_sentence: Tạm biệt, đi đường cẩn thận nha!
example_translation: Goodbye, take care on the road!
notes: Polite and widely used for saying goodbye; not overly formal, so appropriate in most casual and semi-formal situations.

example_sentence: Bye bye, mai gặp lại!
example_translation: Bye bye, see you tomorrow!
notes: An English loanword widely used in Southern Vietnam for informal goodbyes, especially among young people. Avoid it in formal or polite situations.

example_sentence: Ăn cơm chưa? Ăn rồi thì vô nhà chơi đi.
example_translation: Have you eaten yet? If you've eaten, come on in and hang out.
notes: A casual, caring greeting common in the South (and across Vietnam); used among friends and family to ask if someone has eaten and is often rhetorical rather than a literal, formal question.

example_sentence: Chúc ngủ ngon nha, mai mình dậy sớm đi chợ chung.
example_translation: Good night, we'll get up early tomorrow to go to the market together.
notes: Say this to family or friends before bedtime; it's a warm, casual good‑night wish, and in the South people often soften it with friendly, informal particles or tone.

example_sentence: Chúc mừng năm mới! Chúc gia đình mình sức khỏe, phát tài.
example_translation: Happy New Year! Wishing our family health and prosperity.
notes: Common greeting for Tết (Vietnamese Lunar New Year); in the South people often add wishes for health and prosperity (phát tài). Appropriate in both casual and formal settings.

example_sentence: Chúc mừng sinh nhật nha! Mừng tuổi mới gặp nhiều may mắn.
example_translation: Happy birthday! Hope you have lots of luck in your new age.
notes: Use anytime to wish someone a happy birthday—it's neutral and appropriate in most situations. In Southern speech you can add the friendly final particle "nha" to sound warmer and more informal.

example_sentence: Chúc sức khỏe ba mẹ, ăn uống đủ chất nghen.
example_translation: Wishing parents good health, eat well, okay?
notes: Use when wishing good health to older people or in formal greetings (e.g., New Year wishes); it's polite and respectful rather than casual.

example_sentence: A-lô, ai đó? Dạ, em đây nè.
example_translation: Hello, who is it? Yes, it's me.
notes: Used when answering the phone in Vietnam; in the South it's spoken softly and in a friendly, casual tone.

example_sentence: Rất vui được gặp chị hôm nay, em nghe nhiều chuyện hay rồi nè.
example_translation: Very pleased to meet you today, I've heard a lot of good things about you.
notes: Use when meeting someone for the first time; in the South people often use a casual "so happy" instead of the more formal "very pleased." Use appropriate age-/status-based terms for the other person to match formality. | anh = older male (use for men older than you or similar age) | chị = older female (use for women older than you or similar age) | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

english: So glad to see you again
example_sentence: Mừng quá được gặp lại mấy đứa, lâu rồi tụi mình không tụ tập.
example_translation: So happy to see you all again, it's been a while since we hung out.
notes: Used to show joy at reuniting; informal and very natural in Southern Vietnamese speech. Add a casual tag like "you guys" when speaking to close friends or family.

example_sentence: Dạo này sao rồi? Công việc ổn hông?
example_translation: How have you been lately? Is work okay?
notes: An informal, friendly check-in to ask how someone’s been recently; in the South it’s said in a gentle, casual way rather than as a formal greeting.

example_sentence: Thôi mình đi nha, mai gặp lại sớm ha.
example_translation: Alright I'm off, see you again soon tomorrow.
notes: A casual goodbye used when leaving friends; adding "nha" softens it and is typical of Southern speech. | mình = I/me (casual, friendly — used between close friends)

english: Excuse me / Sorry (when entering or interrupting)
example_sentence: Em xin lỗi vô trễ nha, kẹt xe quá.
example_translation: Sorry I'm late, there was heavy traffic.
notes: Common in Southern Vietnamese, use this polite, humble apology when interrupting, entering a room, or asking permission. The pronoun "em" shows the speaker is younger or lower in status—swap it (e.g., to "anh" or "chị") for older or more formal addressees. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Chào mừng anh chị đến nhà, vô nhà ngồi chơi đi.
example_translation: Welcome to our house, come in and sit down.
notes: Used to welcome guests or at events; in Southern Vietnamese you can add "anh" or "chị" to sound more polite and friendly.

example_sentence: Chúc một ngày tốt lành nha, làm việc gì cũng suôn sẻ!
example_translation: Have a nice day, hope everything goes smoothly!
notes: A polite farewell used to wish someone well for the day; appropriate in formal or semi‑formal contexts (emails, customers, elders). In casual Southern speech, people more often use simpler, friendlier expressions.

example_sentence: Chào anh, lâu hông gặp?
example_translation: Hello, long time no see?
notes: Use as a general greeting in everyday situations. In the South speakers often drop the polite word and use a shorter, casual form.

example_sentence: Chào bạn, tên bạn là gì?
example_translation: Hi, what's your name?
notes: Informal and friendly—use with peers or new acquaintances; avoid in formal or respectful situations. | bạn = friend/peer (neutral, same age)

example_sentence: Chào buổi sáng anh, dậy sớm hông?
example_translation: Good morning, did you wake up early?
notes: Use this greeting in the morning. "'Hông' is the Southern, informal pronunciation of 'không' (no/not), so it's casual and regional.

example_sentence: Dạ, em tên là Lan.
example_translation: Yes, my name is Lan.
notes: A polite "yes"/acknowledgement used to show respect to elders or strangers—very common in Southern Vietnam.

example_sentence: Em tên là Minh, rất vui được gặp anh.
example_translation: My name is Minh, nice to meet you.
notes: Use "em" when you're younger than the listener or to sound polite/casual — "Em tên là..." is a friendly Southern way to say "My name is." If the listener is older, use "anh" (to an older man) or "chị" (to an older woman) instead. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Cho em hỏi, bạn tên gì?
example_translation: May I ask, what's your name?
notes: A common, friendly, and polite way to ask someone’s name among people of the same age; it's widely used in the South. When speaking to someone older, swap to the appropriate older-person honorific. | bạn = friend/peer (neutral, same age)

example_sentence: Bạn ở đâu vậy? Em ở Sài Gòn.
example_translation: Where are you from? I'm from Saigon.
notes: A casual way to ask where someone is from; in Southern speech people usually say "Saigon" rather than the formal "Ho Chi Minh City." Use more polite phrasing with elders or in formal situations. | bạn = friend/peer (neutral, same age)

example_sentence: Em đến từ Cần Thơ, hôm nay mới vô Sài Gòn.
example_translation: I'm from Can Tho, I just came to Saigon today.
notes: Use this to say where you’re from—it's a neutral, common way to state your origin. english: What do you do? / What's your job?
example_sentence: Bạn làm nghề gì ở đây?
example_translation: What do you do here?
notes: Ask about someone's occupation — it's neutral but can feel personal, so use it with acquaintances or in appropriate contexts (e.g., networking) rather than with strangers. In Southern speech it's common and sounds casual/polite. | bạn = friend/peer (neutral, same age)

example_sentence: Em làm marketing cho một công ty công nghệ.
example_translation: I work in marketing for a tech company.
notes: Use "I work as..." followed by the job title; in Southern Vietnamese it's common to mix English job titles into Vietnamese sentences, and this usage is casual/informal. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Em là sinh viên, năm hai rồi.
example_translation: I'm a student, I'm in my second year.
notes: Use the word for university/college students when referring to higher education and a different word for schoolchildren. In the South it’s natural to start with a polite, informal first‑person pronoun to sound respectful. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Rất vui được gặp chị, chị dễ thương quá.
example_translation: Nice to meet you, you're so nice.
notes: Use this after introductions to politely say you're glad to meet someone; replace "anh" or "chị" with the appropriate address (anh = older/peer male, chị = older/peer female). example_sentence: Hân hạnh được gặp anh, em là Minh từ công ty XYZ.
example_translation: Pleased to meet you, I'm Minh from company XYZ.
notes: Polite and formal—use it in professional or official meetings. In Southern Vietnam it’s uncommon in casual or friendly conversation. | anh = older male (use for men older than you or similar age) | chị = older female (use for women older than you or similar age)

english: Can I have your phone number?
vietnamese: Cho em xin số điện thoại được hông?

example_sentence: Cho em xin số điện thoại được hông? Em muốn liên lạc.
example_translation: Can I have your phone number? I want to contact you.
notes: A Southern colloquial way to soften a request—polite and warm. Use it with people you already know or when there’s mutual goodwill; it’s casual, so avoid in formal situations. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

english: May I ask... / Excuse me (to start a question)
example_sentence: Cho em hỏi anh tên là gì?
example_translation: May I ask, what's your name?
notes: A polite, soft opening used to start a question with a stranger or service worker—common in the South and by speakers who refer to themselves as "em" (younger or lower status). example_sentence: Cho em tự giới thiệu nha, em là Lan, mới vô làm.
example_translation: Let me introduce myself, I'm Lan, I just started working here.
notes: Adding "nha" softens and makes the line friendly; use it for casual introductions to a group or new colleagues in Southern Vietnam. example_sentence: Đây là bạn của em, tên là Hùng.
example_translation: This is my friend, his name is Hung.

example_sentence: Lâu rồi hông gặp, dạo này sao rồi?
example_translation: Long time no see, how have you been lately?
notes: Common in casual, friendly speech—'hông' is the Southern pronunciation of 'không', so use it with friends or peers, not in formal situations.

example_sentence: Ok, hẹn gặp lại nha, giữ liên lạc.
example_translation: Ok, see you later, keep in touch.
notes: Use when saying goodbye; adding "nha" softens the phrase and makes it sound friendly and casual, common in Southern speech.

example_sentence: Bạn mấy tuổi? Em 24 tuổi rồi.
example_translation: How old are you? I'm 24.
notes: A casual, Southern-style way to ask someone's age. It can be sensitive—especially with strangers or women—so use it cautiously or choose a more polite phrasing. | bạn = friend/peer (neutral, same age)

example_sentence: Bạn có người yêu chưa? Nếu chưa, mai mời đi uống nước.
example_translation: Do you have a partner yet? If not, would you like to go for a drink tomorrow?
notes: Very personal—only ask if you’re close or clearly showing romantic interest; Southern speakers are generally more direct and casual when asking. | bạn = friend/peer (neutral, same age)

vietnamese: Rất vui được quen biết bạn
pronunciation: rut vooy duoc kwen beet bahn
example_sentence: Rất vui được quen biết bạn, hy vọng gặp lại.
example_translation: Nice to know you, hope to see you again.
notes: A slightly more polite/formal way to say "nice to meet you," used to express a good impression when meeting someone new—appropriate for polite introductions. | bạn = friend/peer (neutral, same age)

vietnamese: Xin lỗi, em quên tên rồi
pronunciation: sin loy, em qwen ten roy
example_sentence: Xin lỗi, em quên tên rồi, anh nhắc lại đi.
example_translation: Sorry, I forgot your name, please remind me.
notes: Useful when you meet someone you recently met again—apologizing before asking their name is polite. The phrasing is casual and Southern (using "em" for a younger or familiar person); use "tôi/anh/chị" for more formal situations. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Em nên gọi anh/chị là gì?
pronunciation: em nen goi ahn/chee lah zee?
example_sentence: Em nên gọi chị là gì cho tiện?
example_translation: What should I call you to make it convenient?
notes: Use this to politely ask how someone prefers to be addressed (anh/chị/em) to avoid mistakes—it's a common show of respect in Vietnamese culture; in the South people may be more relaxed, but age and relationship still determine the correct form. | anh = older male (use for men older than you or similar age) | chị = older female (use for women older than you or similar age) | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Cảm ơn anh đã giới thiệu, dạ cảm ơn nhiều.
example_translation: Thank you for the introduction, thank you very much.
notes: Used when someone introduces you or helps you; the usual reply is "you're welcome" or "no problem." It's fine in most situations, and in the South the reply is often said more casually with a relaxed pronunciation.

example_sentence: Xin chào chị, lâu rồi hông gặp!
example_translation: Hello, sister — long time no see!
notes: Use to greet someone; it’s often shortened in casual speech. In the South people tend to be more informal, so you’ll commonly hear the shorter form.

example_sentence: Chào em, đi đâu rứa?
example_translation: Hi, where are you going?
notes: Very common in everyday conversation and more casual/friendly than a formal greeting. "Rứa" is the Southern-dialect pronunciation of "vậy" (meaning "so" / "like that").

example_sentence: Dạ, em hiểu rồi.
example_translation: Yes, I understand.
notes: Use "dạ" as a polite "yes"/acknowledgement to show respect to elders, guests, or in formal situations; in the South it's commonly used in everyday polite speech.

example_sentence: Em hông biết, chị thông cảm nha.
example_translation: I don't know, please understand.
notes: Southern dialect form of "no" used in informal, familiar speech — casual and not suitable for formal writing.

example_sentence: Cảm ơn chị nha, chị tốt quá.
example_translation: Thank you, you're so kind.
notes: A basic, common thank-you; add "nha" to sound friendly/casual (especially in the South), or add "ạ"/"dạ" to be more polite/formal.

example_sentence: Dạ cảm ơn anh đã giúp em.
example_translation: Thank you for helping me.
notes: Add "Dạ" at the start to make your "thank you" more polite; commonly used with elders or customers in Southern Vietnam.

example_sentence: Hông có chi, em làm vui thôi.
example_translation: You're welcome, I was happy to do it.
notes: Casual Southern way to say "you're welcome"; use informally with friends or family—use the more formal standard phrase in polite or official settings.

example_sentence: Xin lỗi nha, em đi lẹ một chút.
example_translation: Sorry, I'm leaving for a bit.
notes: Use this for small mistakes or to get someone's attention; add "ạ" or "dạ" to sound more polite or formal.

example_sentence: Em xin lỗi, em quên mất hẹn với chị.
example_translation: I'm sorry, I forgot our appointment.
notes: Use this when the speaker uses "em" (younger or lower in status) to apologize to someone older or higher—it's a polite, personal apology commonly used in Southern Vietnam. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Xin lỗi đã làm phiền chị, có hơi bận hông?
example_translation: Sorry to bother you, are you a bit busy?
notes: Use this as a polite opener when asking or interrupting someone who might be inconvenienced. In Southern speech it's appropriate in formal or polite situations and is often shortened in casual conversation.

example_sentence: Cho em hỏi, chỗ này bán vé hông?
example_translation: May I ask, does this place sell tickets?
notes: A common, polite opener to request information—'em' signals the speaker is younger or lower-status. example_sentence: Xin phép vô lấy đồ một xíu nha.
example_translation: May I come in to get something briefly?
notes: Use to politely ask permission—e.g., before entering someone's home or doing something that affects others; common when addressing hosts, elders, or in formal situations.

example_sentence: Mời anh vô ngồi đi.
example_translation: Please come in and sit.
notes: Used to politely invite or offer something—e.g., “please come in,” “please sit,” or “please eat.” Very polite and commonly used in Southern Vietnamese.

example_sentence: Mời ngồi, em pha trà cho.
example_translation: Please sit, I'll make tea.
notes: Use when welcoming guests and offering them a seat. "Mời" is a polite, commonly used Southern phrasing by the host and is appropriate in both casual homes and formal settings.

example_sentence: Anh giúp em với được hông? Túi nặng quá.
example_translation: Can you help me? The bag is too heavy.
notes: A casual way to ask for help — add "is that OK?" (Southern speech) to soften the request and ask if it’s possible. example_sentence: Giúp em được hông, cái này khó quá.
example_translation: Could you please help me? This is too hard.
notes: A very natural Southern Vietnamese colloquial tag used to ask permission or make a casual request (e.g., “Could you please help me?”). It’s informal and friendly—use with friends or family and avoid formal or polite situations where more standard phrasing is expected. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Hông sao đâu, em phụ chị được mà.
example_translation: It's okay, I can help you.
notes: Informal phrase to reassure or comfort someone and downplay worry; "hông" is the Southern dialect form of "không" (no/not).

example_sentence: Cảm ơn trước nha nếu anh giúp được vụ này.
example_translation: Thanks in advance if you can help with this.
notes: Use when asking for help—polite and casual (Southern "nha")—but avoid overusing it to pressure people or turn it into a demand.

example_sentence: Xin lỗi, nói lại được hông? Em nghe hông rõ.
example_translation: Sorry, can you repeat? I didn't hear clearly.

example_sentence: Mời chị đi trước đi, em chạy chậm xíu.
example_translation: You go ahead, I'll walk a bit slower.

example_sentence: Em biết ơn lắm vì anh đã tới giúp em hôm nay.

notes: Expresses deeper gratitude than "thank you"—a sincere, emphatic phrase. example_sentence: Hông, cảm ơn, em ổn rồi.

example_sentence: Để em làm cho, chị nghỉ đi.
example_translation: Let me do it for you, please rest.
notes: Use this to volunteer to help someone ("Let me/Allow me"). example_sentence: Chúc mừng chị nha, thành công ghê!
example_translation: Congratulations — what great success!
notes: Use for celebratory occasions—birthdays, graduations, promotions, etc. Add a kinship/title like chị (for an older woman) or anh (for an older man) to sound more familiar.

example_sentence: Hẹn gặp lại nhé, giữ sức khỏe nha.
example_translation: See you again, take care.
notes: A polite goodbye used when you expect to meet again; suitable in formal or neutral situations. In the South people often add a friendly particle (e.g., “nha” or “nhé”) to sound warmer and more casual.

example_sentence: Xe hết pin hông chạy được nửa tiếng, hông em?
example_translation: The bike ran out of battery in less than half an hour, right?
notes: A casual Southern pronunciation used informally for "no" or "zero"—common in everyday speech (including naming the digit 0); use the standard form in formal writing.

example_sentence: Cho em một ly trà đá thôi nha.
example_translation: Just give me one glass of iced tea, please.

example_sentence: Anh cần hai cái vé, dạ.
example_translation: I need two tickets, yes.
notes: Pronounced like English 'hi'. No special southern variant; used in counting and prices.

example_sentence: Gọi ba phần cơm, cho chị nhé.
example_translation: Order three portions of rice for me, please.
notes: Simple cardinal number used everywhere. In Southern speech tone is relaxed.

example_sentence: Số nhà em là bốn, nhưng mấy người hay nói 'tư' cho nhanh.
example_translation: My house number is four, but people often say 'tư' to be quick.
notes: Use bốn in standard or formal contexts; tư is a colloquial Southern variant commonly used after tens (e.g., 24) or in casual speech.

example_sentence: Giá chai nước năm chục nghen, em trả lăm chục hông?
example_translation: The bottle costs fifty, okay? Will you pay fifty?
notes: Use "lăm" when pronouncing numbers where 5 is the final digit after the tens (15, 25, 35...), which is common in Southern speech; "năm" is the base form used alone or in more formal/written contexts.

example_sentence: Sáu giờ tụi mình ăn tối nha.
example_translation: Let's have dinner at six o'clock.
notes: Common cardinal number; pronounced similar to English 'sow'.

example_sentence: Còn bảy phút nữa tới ga, chị ơi.
example_translation: There are seven minutes left until the station, sis.
notes: Used like in English. In fast Southern speech tones are lighter.

example_sentence: Cho em tám cái kem đi, dạ.
example_translation: Give me eight ice creams, please.
notes: Straightforward; used for counting and prices.

example_sentence: Món đó chín ngàn một phần thôi.
example_translation: That dish is only nine thousand per portion.
notes: Common cardinal number; watch final 'n' sound in fast speech.

example_sentence: Mười phút nữa em tới nè.
example_translation: I'll arrive in ten minutes.
notes: Use mười as the base for 11–19 (mười + digit); in Southern Vietnamese it’s often slightly shortened or clipped in casual speech but still easily understood.

example_sentence: Mười hai người vô rồi, còn mười ba nữa là đủ.
example_translation: Twelve people have come in; with thirteen more it'll be enough.
notes: Form 11–19 by saying "ten" + the unit (e.g., "ten one" = 11, "ten two" = 12); Southern speakers often run them together in casual speech and usually use the straightforward "ten one" for 11 rather than the northern variant that substitutes a special word for "one."

example_sentence: Hai mươi, ba mươi, bốn mươi... nói ngắn là hai mươi hả?
example_translation: Twenty, thirty, forty... shortened you say 'hai mươi', right?
notes: Put the tens marker after the digit to form numbers like twenty or thirty. In fast Southern speech this marker is often pronounced like "moy."

example_sentence: Tui mua hai mươi quyển vở cho lớp.
example_translation: I bought twenty notebooks for the class.
notes: This is the standard way to say 20. In Southern speech people often use the informal expression "two tens" to mean "around twenty."

vietnamese: mốt (dùng thay 'một' sau số chục, như 21)
example_sentence: Hai mươi mốt người tới tiệc, hết chỗ ngồi rồi.
example_translation: Twenty-one people came to the party; there's no seat left.
notes: Use "mốt" instead of "một" when saying numbers like 21 or 31 — it's common in spoken Vietnamese, especially in the South. Don't use "mốt" alone; it's only used in compound numbers after tens.

example_sentence: Ba mươi lăm dùa thôi, xài vừa đủ.
example_translation: Thirty-five is enough, just use that.
notes: Use "lăm" instead of "năm" when 5 is the final digit after the tens (e.g., 25 → "lăm"). This form is required in speech and very common in the South; in formal writing you may still see "năm."

example_sentence: Trăm đồng giờ ít có giá trị, mấy em biết hông?
example_translation: A hundred dong isn't worth much now, you know?
notes: Place the word for "hundred" after a numeral (e.g., two hundred = 200). In Southern Vietnamese casual speech, sounds are often shortened, so spoken forms may sound clipped.

example_sentence: Cái áo kia giá một ngàn hai trăm, rẻ đó nha.
example_translation: That shirt costs 1,200, quite cheap.
notes: Both mean "thousand"; Southern speakers often use ngàn in casual speech, while nghìn is slightly more formal or common in writing.

example_sentence: Nhà đang bán hai tỷ, tức là hai ngàn triệu, chứ hông phải chơi đâu.
example_translation: The house is being sold for two billion, meaning two thousand millions, it's no joke.
notes: In Southern Vietnamese everyday speech, people talk about money informally and often mix million and billion when stating amounts. Use a casual southern tone rather than formal wording.

example_sentence: Căn nhà đó định giá hơn một tỷ rồi.
example_translation: That house is priced at over one billion already.
notes: "Tỷ" means one billion (10^9); you'll hear it often in real estate, finance, and everyday talk about large sums. It's a neutral, standard term used across Vietnam, including the South.

vietnamese: thứ + (nhất, hai, ba...) — sắp xếp thứ tự
example_sentence: Hội thi xếp hạng rồi: thí sinh thứ nhất là Huỳnh, dạ hổng có gì to tát.
example_translation: The contest ranked them: the first contestant is Huynh, it's not a big deal.
notes: Put "thứ" before a number to make ordinals (thứ nhất = first); it's the neutral way to show order. In casual Southern speech, people often use "hạng nhất" to mean "first place" or top-ranked in informal/ranking contexts.

example_sentence: Cho em nửa ký thôi, đủ ăn rồi.
example_translation: Give me just half a kilo, that's enough to eat.
notes: Used to mean half, often with or without the word "one" in everyday speech (e.g., half an hour). In Southern Vietnamese it's pronounced softly—like "nuh"—and is typically casual.

example_sentence: Mấy đứa đó đi hông?
example_translation: Are those kids going or not?
notes: Use this word to ask "how many" about a small, unspecified number (e.g., "how many people?"). It's very common in Southern speech and casual; speakers from other regions may use a different, more neutral term.

vietnamese: bao nhiêu (hỏi con số hoặc giá cả)
example_sentence: Cái này giá bao nhiêu tiền? Dạ bao nhiêu hả chị?
example_translation: How much does this cost? — How much is it, sis?
notes: Use to ask for a quantity or a price. In Southern casual speech the full "how much" question is often shortened—these clipped forms are common, casual, and widely understood.

vietnamese: chục (nghĩa là mấy chục, hàng chục)
example_sentence: Tui mua chục trái táo là đủ, hông cần nhiều.
example_translation: I'll buy around ten apples; that's enough, no need for many.
notes: Informal, casual term meaning "about ten" or "a few tens" (i.e., dozens) used when rounding or estimating quantities. Very common in everyday Southern Vietnamese speech.

example_sentence: Anh ơi, mấy giờ rồi?
example_translation: Hey, what time is it?
notes: A very familiar, everyday way to ask the time; in the South people say it simply without adding "không" at the end. Use with friends and family, not in formal situations.

example_sentence: Bây giờ tụi mình đi được hông?
example_translation: Can we go now?
notes: Commonly used when asking about the present moment; "tụi mình" is a Southern, casual way to say "we/us."

example_sentence: Hôm nay em bận hông?
example_translation: Are you busy today?
notes: Very common: in Southern Vietnamese, a colloquial short form of "no/not" is used in questions, so it's casual and used in everyday speech.

example_sentence: Ngày mai mình đi chơi được hông?
example_translation: Can we go out tomorrow?
notes: Use "mình" as a casual, friendly "I" common in Southern Vietnam. Southern speakers also often add "hông" at the end of a sentence to make a yes/no question.

example_sentence: Hôm qua anh có tới hông?
example_translation: Did you come yesterday?
notes: Used to talk about a past time. In Southern Vietnam speakers often add kinship words like "anh/chị/em" to sound more friendly or intimate.

example_sentence: Tui dậy sớm mỗi buổi sáng.
example_translation: I wake up early every morning.
notes: "Tui" is the Southern casual equivalent of "I," used with friends/family; "buổi sáng" refers to the morning period from early dawn until around noon.

example_sentence: Chiều nay rảnh hông?
example_translation: Are you free this afternoon?
notes: Refers to the time from after noon until early evening and is commonly used when scheduling appointments. It's neutral in register; in Southern casual speech people often use a shorter form.

example_sentence: Tối nay đi ăn hông?
example_translation: Do you want to go eat tonight?
notes: Refers to the time after sunset; in Southern speech invitations using "buổi tối" are usually very short and informal—friendly and casual, as in the example.

example_sentence: Đêm qua mưa dữ hông?
example_translation: It rained heavily last night, didn't it?
notes: Use this word for the late-night hours through early morning. In Southern speech, an informal intensifier meaning "very" is commonly added to emphasize degree (it's casual).

example_sentence: Tui tới nửa đêm mới về.
example_translation: I only got home at midnight.
notes: Use to refer to around 12:00 AM (the middle of the night); it's a neutral, common term in Southern Vietnamese speech and writing.

example_sentence: Trưa mình ăn uống chỗ nào?
example_translation: Where should we eat at noon?
notes: Refers to midday (about 11:00–13:00). In Southern Vietnamese people commonly use short, casual phrases to say "have lunch."

example_sentence: Cuộc họp bắt đầu 3 giờ nha.
example_translation: The meeting starts at 3 o'clock.
notes: Use the word for "o'clock" to state the hour; in Southern speech you can drop the word equivalent to "at" and just say the number + "o'clock" (e.g. 3 o'clock). This is neutral and common in everyday conversation.

example_sentence: Hẹn 2 giờ rưỡi nha.
example_translation: Let's meet at 2:30, okay?
notes: Place after the hour to mean “half past” (e.g., 2 giờ rưỡi = 2:30). It's very common and brief in Southern Vietnamese, used in everyday speech.

vietnamese: Mười lăm phút (ví dụ: 1 giờ mười lăm)
pronunciation: moo-ee lam foot (e.g., one zuh moo-ee lam)
example_sentence: Buổi học bắt đầu 1 giờ mười lăm.
example_translation: The class starts at 1:15.
notes: In everyday conversation people usually say "mười lăm phút" (fifteen minutes) rather than the more formal "một phần tư."

vietnamese: Kém mười lăm (ví dụ: 3 giờ kém mười lăm)
example_sentence: 3 giờ kém mười lăm là mấy giờ vậy?
example_translation: What time is 3 minus fifteen minutes (i.e., 2:45)?
notes: Use this to indicate how many minutes are left before the next hour (e.g., 3 o'clock minus 10 minutes = 2:50). It's common in everyday speech across Vietnam, including the South, and is neutral in register.

example_sentence: Chờ 5 phút thôi.
example_translation: Wait just 5 minutes.
notes: Use for short durations; in Southern Vietnamese casual speech people often shorten numbers and add a particle meaning "just" (e.g., "five minutes only") to sound informal.

example_sentence: Chờ 1 giây nha, xíu tui nói liền.
example_translation: Wait one second, I'll speak in a moment.
notes: The term for "second" is uncommon in everyday speech except when stressing a very brief, precise moment. In Southern Vietnamese, people usually use a casual word meaning "a little/a moment" in informal contexts.

example_sentence: Ngày mai có mưa hông?
example_translation: Will it rain tomorrow?
notes: Use 'ngày' to refer to a specific day or calendar date. In Southern speech, yes/no questions often end with "hông," so asking about the day sounds more casual if you add that particle.

example_sentence: Tuần sau rảnh hông?
example_translation: Are you free next week?
notes: Means "week"; Southern Vietnamese commonly use it in phrases like "this week," "next week," and "last week" — it's neutral and used in everyday, casual speech.

example_sentence: Cuối tuần mình đi biển nha.
example_translation: Let's go to the beach this weekend.
notes: It means "weekend" — in Southern Vietnam people commonly say "go out on the weekend" to refer to casual leisure outings; it's informal, everyday speech.

example_sentence: Tháng sau tui đi Cần Thơ.
example_translation: Next month I'm going to Cần Thơ.
notes: Use "tháng" to refer to calendar (solar/Gregorian) months. "Tui" and "mình" are informal, Southern Vietnamese pronouns used in casual speech among friends.

example_sentence: Năm sau mình đi du lịch nha.
example_translation: Let's travel next year, okay?
notes: Means the Gregorian calendar year. In the South, people naturally use it in phrases for "this year" and "next year," in both casual and neutral contexts.

example_sentence: Cho tui coi lịch coi ngày đi.
example_translation: Let me see the calendar to check the date.
notes: "Lịch" can mean a wall calendar, a digital calendar, or an appointment schedule. "Coi ngày" means to check a specific date (often to pick an auspicious or lucky day); "coi" is a Southern colloquialism for "xem" (to look/check).

example_sentence: Em có hẹn bác sĩ mấy giờ?
example_translation: What time is your appointment with the doctor?
notes: Use this common word for any kind of meeting or appointment. In the South people often add a casual friendly tag when arranging plans, so it’s informal—use more formal phrasing for official appointments.

example_sentence: Anh tới đúng giờ nha, đừng trễ. Nếu trễ thì gọi cho em; em sẽ tới sớm.
example_translation: Please arrive on time, don't be late. If you're late call me; I'll come early.
notes: Use for appointments, meetings, and formal events—it's a neutral term. In the South, a slight delay is often tolerated socially among friends, but aim to be on time for work or official commitments.

example_sentence: Cái áo này bao nhiêu tiền dzậy?
example_translation: How much is this shirt?
notes: Use this daily to ask the price at markets or shops. In the South sellers usually reply directly, and buyers often add a casual, friendly particle to sound more familiar.

example_sentence: Đắt quá, em không mua đâu.
example_translation: It's too expensive, I won't buy it.
notes: Use this casual phrase to complain about price; in Southern speech people sometimes use a different colloquial variant, but this expression is the most common and natural.

example_sentence: Rẻ quá, mua đi chị!
example_translation: So cheap, buy it sis!
notes: Use to praise a good price or encourage someone to buy; it's casual and commonly heard in Southern markets and street stalls.

example_sentence: Em có tiền lẻ hông? Mình cần vài tờ lẻ để trả.
example_translation: Do you have small change? We need some small bills to pay.
notes: Use when you need small-denomination bills or coins—commonly said when buying single items or paying a taxi; neutral, everyday Southern usage.

example_sentence: Cho em tiền thừa nè, khỏi cần anh giữ giùm.
example_translation: Here's your change, you don't need to keep it for me.
notes: Use when receiving change after paying; this casual Southern expression is commonly used by vendors and in small shops or markets.

example_sentence: Cho em xin hóa đơn với được hông?
example_translation: Can I get the receipt, please?
notes: Use this to ask for a purchase invoice needed for tax refunds, warranties, or record‑keeping; in Southern Vietnam staff will often reply with the polite acknowledgement "dạ."

example_sentence: Anh ơi, tính tiền cho tụi em với!
example_translation: Excuse me, can we get the bill please!
notes: A common way to ask for the bill at a restaurant; you can add a casual softener to sound friendlier, as is typical in everyday Southern speech.

example_sentence: Bớt được hông chị? Giá còn hơi cao quá.
example_translation: Can you lower the price? It's a bit expensive.
notes: A casual, friendly bargaining line for markets and small shops; in Southern Vietnam people often add a short softening filler to make it more polite. Use with vendors or acquaintances—avoid it in formal or upscale settings.

vietnamese: Thanh toán bằng thẻ được hông?
pronunciation: than toan bang the duoc hong
example_sentence: Em thanh toán bằng thẻ được hông? Không có tiền mặt đâu.
example_translation: Can I pay by card? I don't have cash.
notes: Casual Southern way to ask if a shop accepts card—use it in everyday situations. In Saigon many places take cards, but small markets and street vendors often still prefer cash.

example_sentence: Tôi trả tiền mặt, em giữ tiền lẻ lại nha.
example_translation: I'll pay cash, please keep the small change.
notes: Cards are common, but cash is still widely used—especially at markets, small shops, and street-side stalls; carry some for everyday purchases.

example_sentence: Anh gửi tiền cho em bằng chuyển khoản được hông?
example_translation: Can you transfer the money to me by bank transfer?
notes: Commonly used for online buying/selling and sending money between family; always confirm the recipient’s account number and the transfer description/purpose before sending.

example_sentence: Gần đây có cây ATM hông? Em muốn rút tiền mặt.
example_translation: Is there an ATM nearby? I want to withdraw cash.
notes: In the South, people commonly use the casual term "ATM." Be aware some machines charge a fee if you withdraw with a card from another bank.

example_sentence: Giá niêm yết trên đó rồi, em xem kỹ nha.
example_translation: The posted price is over there, check it carefully.
notes: Used in supermarkets or shops with official price tags — don’t haggle if the price is posted; at local markets you can negotiate when no price is displayed.

example_sentence: Đang giảm giá 20% đó, mau lên chị!
example_translation: It's 20% off now, hurry up sis!
notes: Use this for discounts in ads, signs, or when asking about price reductions; it's often paired with “promotion” (khuyến mãi) in marketing. In Southern Vietnam sales pitches are typically upbeat and friendly, so expect casual, energetic wording rather than formal language.

example_sentence: Ăn xong mình chia tiền nha, mỗi người trả một ít.
example_translation: After eating let's split the bill, each person pays a bit.
notes: Use when splitting the cost at a group meal; in the South people often borrow the English word "bill," but the native expression is considered purer—both are casual and used with friends.

example_sentence: Anh có thể cho em mượn tiền tạm được hông?
example_translation: Can you lend me some money temporarily?
notes: Use with acquaintances or friends; borrowing money is treated delicately in Vietnam because it affects relationships and personal reputation.

example_sentence: Em còn nợ anh bao nhiêu rồi? Nhắc em trả nha.
example_translation: How much do I still owe you? Remind me to pay back.
notes: Used for informal "put it on my tab" situations at small neighborhood shops or regular eateries; in the South shopkeepers often record debts in a notebook or just remember verbal arrangements with regular customers.

example_sentence: Lương tháng này em được tăng một ít.
example_translation: My salary this month increased a bit.
notes: Used to talk about income. In the South, asking "How much do you earn?" is considered delicate and usually only asked directly of close friends; it's informal.

example_sentence: Em đang tiết kiệm tiền để mua xe máy.
example_translation: I'm saving money to buy a motorbike.
notes: Used for personal financial planning. In Southern speech people often say "collect money" to mean slowly putting money aside — casual usage.

example_sentence: Em muốn đổi đô sang tiền Việt, chỗ nào tốt hông?
example_translation: I want to exchange dollars to VND, is there a good place?
notes: In Southern Vietnam people commonly use a casual phrase to mean "exchange US dollars"; always ask about the exchange rate and any fees before converting money.

example_sentence: Ví của em bị rơi, em tìm không thấy tiền rồi.
example_translation: My wallet fell and I can't find the money.
notes: Very common; if you lose your wallet, usually tell the owner so it can be returned or contact the police depending on the situation.

example_sentence: Ăn xong em để lại chút tiền boa cho phục vụ.
example_translation: After eating I left a small tip for the server.
notes: Tipping isn’t required in Vietnam, but leaving a small amount at restaurants, hotels, or for good service is polite; in the South people commonly use the casual short form “boa.”

example_sentence: Phí rút tiền cao quá, đắt hơn rút ở ngân hàng mình.
example_translation: The withdrawal fee is too high, more expensive than withdrawing at our bank.
notes: Check the fee schedule before withdrawing — interbank ATM withdrawals often incur a fee. To save on charges, many people withdraw larger amounts less frequently.

example_sentence: Giá một ký xoài là bao nhiêu?
example_translation: What's the price for one kilogram of mangoes?
notes: Use this to ask the price per unit (one piece, one kilogram, one bottle, etc.). At markets, always clarify whether you mean one kilogram or the whole item so vendors know what you want.

example_sentence: Sản phẩm bị lỗi, cửa hàng hoàn tiền cho em được hông?
example_translation: The product is defective, can the store refund my money?
notes: Use this at stores to request money back for returns, exchanges, or defective items; many places require a receipt, so ask about the return/refund policy first. The phrase is neutral and suitable in both casual and formal settings.

example_sentence: Cho em hỏi, còn bàn trống hông?
example_translation: Excuse me, are there any free tables?
notes: Use to get a server’s attention or ask a question—polite but informal; "em" is a friendly Southern pronoun and "hông" is a casual Southern form of "không." | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Cho em một bàn cho hai người được hông?
pronunciation: cho em mot ban cho hai ngoo-ee duoc hong
example_sentence: Cho em một bàn cho hai người được hông? Em có đặt trước hông.
example_translation: A table for two, please. I didn't reserve, is that okay?
notes: Add "được hông" to soften the request — polite but casual, typical Southern speech. "Cho em" is usually used by a female or younger speaker; a male can say "cho anh" if he prefers. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Em gọi trước rồi, cho em hỏi có đặt chỗ hông?
example_translation: I reserved earlier, may I ask if the reservation is there?
notes: Staff usually asks this when guests arrive at a restaurant or hotel; it's casual Southern speech—'có' sounds like "gaw" and 'hông' is the informal Southern form of 'không' (use "Có đặt chỗ không?" for more formal situations).

vietnamese: Cho em coi thực đơn với
pronunciation: cho em coy thook doon voi
example_sentence: Cho em coi thực đơn với, em muốn xem mấy món đặc biệt.
example_translation: May I see the menu, please? I want to check the specials.
notes: In Southern Vietnamese, "coi" is the informal equivalent of "xem" — use it when asking to see something like a menu. Adding "với" at the end softens the request and makes it feel casual and friendly, suitable for polite interaction with restaurant staff. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Giới thiệu em mấy món ngon với
pronunciation: zoy tee-ow em may mon ngon voi
example_sentence: Anh ơi, giới thiệu em mấy món ngon với, em thích món không quá cay.
example_translation: Hey, recommend me some good dishes—I'd like something not too spicy.
notes: Use casually with familiar staff or the owner, and tell them your preferences (e.g., “not too spicy”) so they can recommend the right dishes. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Cho em gọi món: phở tái một tô, thêm rau sống.
example_translation: I'd like to order: one bowl of rare-beef pho, extra herbs.
notes: A gentle, polite Southern way to call the server and say you'd like to order; the pronoun implies a younger or lower-status speaker (often female). Add "dạ" at the start to sound more courteous. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

english: Can you make it less spicy?
vietnamese: Cho em làm ít cay được hông?
pronunciation: cho em lam it cay duoc hong
example_sentence: Món này cay hông? Nếu cay quá cho em làm ít cay được hông?
example_translation: Is this spicy? If it's too spicy, could you make it less spicy?
notes: Use this at Vietnamese restaurants to ask for milder spice — it's a common, polite Southern Vietnamese way to request less heat. The casual question ending is fine with servers or friends; use a more formal phrasing and pronoun with strangers or in formal situations. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Cho em hông bột ngọt nha
pronunciation: cho em hong bot ngot nha
example_sentence: Em bị dị ứng bột ngọt, cho em hông bột ngọt nha.
example_translation: I'm allergic to MSG, please don't put any MSG.
notes: If needed, state the reason (e.g., an allergy) so staff take it seriously; adding "nha" softens the request and sounds friendly and casual in Southern Vietnamese. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Cho em cái đũa với muỗng nĩa
pronunciation: cho em kai dua voit mooong nyah
example_sentence: Cho em cái đũa với muỗng nĩa, em thích ăn bằng muỗng hơn.
example_translation: Chopsticks and a fork/spoon, please. I prefer eating with a spoon.
notes: Many places already leave them out, but it’s best to ask if you need them. Use "cái" as the classifier for a specific utensil or one set. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Cho em ly nước lọc với
pronunciation: cho em lee nook loc voi
example_sentence: Cho em ly nước lọc với, dạ cảm ơn.
example_translation: A glass of plain water, please. Yes, thank you.
notes: Use "nước lọc" to ask for plain water at restaurants; it's the common phrasing. In the South, people often say "dạ" as a polite "yes" or acknowledgment. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Cho em thêm nước được hông?
pronunciation: cho em them nook duoc hong
example_sentence: Ly nước hết rồi, cho em thêm nước được hông?
example_translation: My glass is empty, could I have a refill?
notes: Casual Southern phrasing for asking staff or friends for a refill—avoid in very formal situations. Small local eateries usually refill quickly (often free), but bigger restaurants may charge separately for bottled water. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Cái này có cay hông? Em ăn cay yếu.
example_translation: Is this spicy? I'm not good with spicy food.
notes: Use when you want to ask if a dish is spicy but aren’t sure; the phrase literally points to "this" dish, and the final particle "hông" is a Southern colloquial marker that makes it casual.

vietnamese: Cho em mang về được hông?
pronunciation: cho em mang vay duoc hong
example_sentence: Ăn chưa hết, cho em mang về được hông?
example_translation: I haven't finished, can I take it to go?
notes: In the South both verbs meaning “to take away” are used; this is a casual way to ask for food to-go, and many places will offer or ask if you want a takeaway box. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Cho em tính tiền, chia ra được hông?
example_translation: Could we get the bill, please? Can we split it?
notes: This phrase is the common, casual way to ask for the bill in Southern Vietnam. At street stalls, customers often bring their money to the counter themselves, and adding a “for me” ending is a friendly, polite way to address the server. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Nhóm em tính riêng, chia tiền ra được hông?
example_translation: Our group will pay separately, can we split the bill?
notes: Informal Southern phrasing — useful to ask in casual eateries, but many small places don’t split bills easily and staff may insist on paying per person, so clarify before you order.

example_sentence: Cho em hỏi, quán có nhận thẻ hông hay chỉ tiền mặt?
example_translation: Do you accept cards or cash only?
notes: Many small shops in southern Vietnam still prefer cash, so ask before paying to avoid hassle. This is an informal Southern way to ask whether they accept cards.

vietnamese: Có bao gồm phí phục vụ hông?
pronunciation: gaw bao goom fee fook voo hong
example_sentence: Hóa đơn có bao gồm phí phục vụ hông? Nếu có cho em biết nha.
example_translation: Does the bill include a service charge? Please let me know if it does.
notes: Big restaurants usually add a 5–10% service charge; small, low‑cost places usually don’t. In the South people rarely tip extra, and this uses an informal Southern question‑tag—use it with servers or friends but not in formal situations.

vietnamese: Nhà vệ sinh ở chỗ mô?
pronunciation: nya vay sin oh chaw mo
example_sentence: Anh ơi, nhà vệ sinh ở chỗ mô? Em cần dùng tí.
example_translation: Where's the restroom? I need to use it for a bit.
notes: Use "chỗ mô" in Southern Vietnamese to mean "where"; add "anh ơi" (to a man) or "chị ơi" (to a woman) before your question to politely call a staff member.

example_sentence: Món này ngon dữ lắm, cảm ơn chị nha!
example_translation: This is really delicious, thank you!
notes: In Southern Vietnamese this adds strong emphasis (“very”). Use the phrase to warmly praise food or staff in casual settings; people often follow it by saying “thank you.”

example_sentence: Món này mặn quá, giúp em bớt muối được hông?
example_translation: This is too salty; could you reduce the salt, please?
notes: Use this gently to tell staff a dish is too salty/sweet; it's casual and commonly used in the South. Restaurant staff will usually try to adjust it if possible.

example_sentence: Em bị dị ứng với tôm, làm ơn cho em món không có tôm nha.
example_translation: I'm allergic to shrimp; please give me a dish without shrimp.
notes: Always state allergies clearly and repeat them to both the server and the chef for dishes that may be mixed or cross‑contaminated. In Southern Vietnamese, using "em" is a polite/neutral self-reference; for severe allergies, explicitly say it's life‑threatening so staff take it seriously. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

english: Can I order this dish again?
vietnamese: Cho em gọi lại món này được hông?
pronunciation: cho em goi lai mon nay duoc hong
example_sentence: Món này ngon quá, cho em gọi lại một phần nữa được hông?
example_translation: This is so good; may I order another portion of it?
notes: Use this to ask a server to reorder the same dish; "cho em" is a polite-young speaker form and "được hông" is casual Southern speech—friendly/informal, so choose a more formal phrasing in formal settings. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Cho em hỏi, quán có Wi‑Fi hông? Em cần check công việc tí.
example_translation: Do you have Wi‑Fi? I need to check some work.
notes: This is a casual, Southern-style way to ask for Wi‑Fi. In Ho Chi Minh City and Cần Thơ many cafés/shops offer free Wi‑Fi and staff will give you the password if available.

english: Do you have a high chair / kids' seat?
example_sentence: Em đưa con đi ăn, quán có ghế cho bé hông?
example_translation: I'm bringing a child—do you have a high chair?
notes: This is a casual Southern way to ask staff; larger restaurants usually have high chairs, but small shops or street stalls may not. "Bé" means child.

example_sentence: Cho em hỏi, quán có món chay hông? Em ăn chay hôm nay.
example_translation: Do you have vegetarian dishes? I'm eating vegetarian today.
notes: Many places serve at least a few vegetarian dishes, but Vietnamese food often uses fish sauce and animal fat—if you’re strictly vegetarian, make it clear “no fish sauce / not fried in lard.”

english: Can I have the same sauce/side?
vietnamese: Cho em lấy thêm cái nước chấm/đồ ăn kèm được hông?
pronunciation: cho em lay them kai nook cham / do an kem duoc hong
example_sentence: Cho em lấy thêm cái nước chấm với, cái này ngon quá.
example_translation: Could I get extra dipping sauce/side? This one is really good.
notes: Use this casual Southern request to ask for extra dipping sauce, herbs, or side dishes at restaurants or street stalls; staff will often give these free or charge only a small fee. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Cho em một ly cà phê sữa đá
pronunciation: cho em moht lee gah feh sue-ah dah
example_sentence: Cho em một ly cà phê sữa đá, đường ít nha.
example_translation: I'll have one iced milk coffee, less sugar please.
notes: In Southern Vietnam, people often use a friendly "give me" phrasing to order—it's casual but polite toward staff. To request less sugar, put "sugar" before "less" (the Southern word order) rather than saying "less sugar." | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Cho anh ly cà phê đen đá được hông?
example_translation: Can I get an iced black coffee?
notes: Use "black" to order coffee with no milk. A common Southern informal question meaning "Can you do that?" or "Is that OK?" is a casual, friendly way to check if something can be done.

example_sentence: Quán có cà phê phin nóng không?
example_translation: Do you have hot phin coffee?
notes: Traditional coffee brewed in a small metal drip filter; in southern Vietnam cafés it’s commonly served hot or with sweetened condensed milk — ask for it iced if you want it cold.

example_sentence: Cho em một ly cà phê sữa nóng, ít đường nha.
example_translation: One hot milk coffee with less sugar, please.
notes: Use when you want your coffee served hot. In the South people often add the softening particle "nha" to make the request more casual/polite.

vietnamese: Có đá / Không đá (hông có đá)
pronunciation: co dah / hong dah (hong co dah)
example_sentence: Ly này có đá hay không đá anh?
example_translation: Is this served with ice or without ice?
notes: Use "with ice" or "no ice" when ordering drinks; in Southern Vietnam people often say a casual, shortened form of "no," so you'll hear informal pronunciation in everyday speech.

example_sentence: Cho em cà phê đậm một chút được hông?
example_translation: Can you make my coffee a bit stronger?
notes: Used to ask for a stronger (more concentrated) or weaker/milder brew—also to specify how milky or thick you want it—when ordering coffee; casual, everyday Southern Vietnamese phrasing.

example_sentence: Em muốn ngọt vừa thôi, đừng ngọt quá nha.
example_translation: I want it moderately sweet, not too sweet.
notes: In Southern Vietnam people commonly say "less sugar" (you may also hear the words in reversed order) in casual speech. Always state a specific sweetness level (e.g., 30% or 50%) because cafes/shops usually follow preset sugar ratios.

example_sentence: Cho em một ly mang đi, gói kỹ dùm nha.
example_translation: One to-go please, please pack it carefully.
notes: Use "to‑go" or "take‑away" for orders you’ll take out—both expressions are common and interchangeable in the South. "For here" means you’ll stay and drink/eat inside; it's a neutral, casual phrasing used in cafés and restaurants.

example_sentence: Mấy phút nữa xong ly của em hông?
example_translation: How many minutes until my drink is ready?
notes: Use this when waiting for something to be ready (e.g., food or an order); it’s casual, and in the South people say "hông" instead of the standard "không."

vietnamese: Thanh toán bằng thẻ được hông?
pronunciation: tinh twaan bang the duoc hong
example_sentence: Anh ơi, thanh toán bằng thẻ được hông?
example_translation: Hey, can I pay by card?
notes: Many small cafés only take cash, so ask before ordering to avoid awkwardness. The phrasing is casual Southern Vietnamese—use it in informal settings or with friendly staff, not in formal situations.

example_sentence: Quán có wifi hông, cho em pass được không?
example_translation: Does the cafe have Wi‑Fi? Can you give me the password?
notes: Locals often use the English loanword "pass" (or "password") when asking for Wi‑Fi—especially in Saigon—so it's a casual, widely understood way to request the network key.

example_sentence: Cho em tính tiền được chưa anh?
example_translation: Can I pay now?
notes: A polite way to ask for the bill—use it when speaking to waitstaff or a cashier. It’s common in Southern speech and uses a pronoun that marks the speaker as younger or female, so it’s informal but respectful. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Còn chỗ ngồi trong quán hông, em với bạn vào được hông?
example_translation: Are there any seats in the cafe? Can my friend and I sit inside?
notes: Use this at a busy café or restaurant to politely ask if seats are available. "Hông" is the Southern casual form of "không," and "được hông?" softens the request to mean "is that okay/available?"

example_sentence: Em muốn giữ chỗ cho tối nay, giữ được hông?
example_translation: I want to reserve a table for tonight, is that possible?
notes: Casual Southern phrasing — specify the time and number of people; many small eateries will take reservations by phone.

example_sentence: Cho em ly nước lọc với, em uống kèm cà phê nha.
example_translation: A glass of water, please — I'll have it with my coffee.
notes: A casual, polite way to ask for a glass of plain water — "nước lọc" means plain water. In the South, cafes and eateries often provide plain water free or included with a meal. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Cho em thêm sữa đặc vô ly cà phê, ngọt hơn xíu nha.
example_translation: Add more condensed milk to my coffee, a bit sweeter please.
notes: Southerners often drink coffee with sweetened condensed milk, so asking for extra is common. "Vô" is the Southern, informal form of "vào" and is natural in casual speech.

example_sentence: Cho em ít đá thôi, đừng có nhiều quá nha.
example_translation: Less ice please, not too much.
notes: Use this phrase when ordering to ask for less ice so your drink won’t get diluted; add a friendly sentence-ending particle (common in Southern casual speech) to sound more polite and relaxed.

example_sentence: Cho anh cà phê không đường, đậm được hông?
example_translation: Black coffee without sugar, can it be strong?
notes: "Hông" is the Southern colloquial form of "không" — say "hông đường" to request no sugar in a drink; it's casual and common in the South, less appropriate for formal situations.

english: Do you have specialty coffee / egg coffee?
vietnamese: Có cà phê đặc sản / cà phê trứng hông?
pronunciation: co kah feh dak san / kah feh chung hong
example_sentence: Quán có cà phê trứng không? Em muốn thử một ly.
example_translation: Do you have egg coffee? I want to try one.
notes: Egg coffee is usually found at specialty coffee shops, so ask first since not every café serves it. Use the casual Southern "hông" — it's informal/colloquial.

english: Is there an outlet to charge my phone?
example_sentence: Cho em ngồi gần chỗ có sạc được hông, em còn pin ít thôi.
example_translation: Can I sit near a power outlet? My battery is low.
notes: Use this casual Southern phrasing to ask staff for a power outlet — the ending is a regional informal question marker. Customers commonly use it in cafés, especially Wi‑Fi spots, when they need to charge devices.

example_sentence: Gói mang đi cho em ly này với, em bận xíu.
example_translation: Pack this to go for me, I'm a bit busy.
notes: Use when asking staff to pack food or drinks to take away; in Southern Vietnamese "cho em" is a casual, polite way to address the server. Staff will usually seal the cup or put the item into a bag or box. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

english: Can you change condensed milk to fresh milk?
vietnamese: Có thể thay sữa đặc bằng sữa tươi được hông?
pronunciation: co teh thay sue-ah dak bang sue-ah toy duoc hong
example_sentence: Cho em cà phê sữa, mà thay sữa đặc bằng sữa tươi được hông?
example_translation: Can you replace condensed milk with fresh milk in my coffee?
notes: Casual Southern phrasing for ordering in cafes — ask first, since some places charge extra for fresh milk.

english: Excuse me, is this mine? (order pick-up)
vietnamese: Xin lỗi, ly này của em hông?
pronunciation: sin loy, lee nay cua em hong
example_sentence: Xin lỗi, ly cà phê này của em hông, em gọi tên…
example_translation: Excuse me, is this my drink? I ordered under the name...
notes: Use this casual Southern phrasing when confirming an order at a café or food stall (e.g., when staff calls or marks your cup). Begin with "Excuse me" to be polite; the Southern question particle is an informal yes/no tag common in everyday speech. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Có thể cho đá sau được hông?
pronunciation: co teh cho dah sow duoc hong
example_sentence: Ly này cho ít đá, mà có thể cho đá sau khi uống nóng xuống được hông?
example_translation: Can you add ice later?
notes: Use this casual Southern phrasing to ask a vendor to serve your drink hot and add ice later—ask before they prepare it so staff can set ice aside. "Hông" is informal (Southern "không"), so use it with friends or casual cafés; say "được không?" to be polite.

example_sentence: Ly này giá bao nhiêu vậy anh?
example_translation: How much is this?
notes: Use this to ask the price. In small shops prices are often posted, but it's perfectly normal to ask the staff.

example_sentence: Anh ơi, cho em xin giá cái này được hông?
example_translation: Excuse me, can you give me the price of this?
notes: Use to get a shopkeeper’s or staff member’s attention in markets or stores; in Southern Vietnam people often call out with familial titles (literally “older brother/sister”) instead of saying “excuse me,” which is casual but polite. | anh = older male (use for men older than you or similar age) | chị = older female (use for women older than you or similar age)

example_sentence: Chị ơi, cái váy này bao nhiêu tiền?
example_translation: Miss, how much is this dress?
notes: A basic, casual question for asking the price; expect haggling and immediate lower offers at street markets, while supermarkets have fixed prices.

english: Can you lower the price? / Can you give me a discount?
example_sentence: Cái túi mắc quá, bớt giá được hông chị?
example_translation: This bag is expensive, can you give a discount?
notes: Use when bargaining at markets or small shops—it's casual Southern speech (hông = không) and not appropriate in big stores/supermarkets where prices are fixed. A friendly tone and smile help when asking for a discount.

example_sentence: Mắc quá, em không mua đâu.
example_translation: It's too expensive, I won't buy it.
notes: Use to refuse a price in informal situations (street markets, bargaining); Southern speakers often add a question-tag or softening particle at the end to make it gentler, so it sounds like "It's too expensive, I won't buy."

english: I'll buy it / I'll take it
example_sentence: Được, em mua liền cái này nhen.
example_translation: Alright, I'll buy this right away.
notes: Use this to say you’ll buy something immediately; it’s casual Southern Vietnamese. Add the speaker’s appropriate personal pronoun to show who’s buying and the level of politeness. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

english: Let me think / I'll think about it
example_sentence: Cái này đẹp nhưng để em coi đã nha.
example_translation: This is nice but let me think first.
notes: A polite Southern-Vietnamese way to say you need time to decide (often used when thinking about a purchase); "coi" is the Southern dialect form of "xem" (to look/consider). | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Cho em thử đồ được hông?
example_sentence: Cái áo này em muốn thử, cho em thử đồ được hông?
example_translation: I want to try this shirt on, can I try it?
notes: Casual Southern way to ask to try clothes—friendly and informal, often used by younger speakers. In small shops you can often try items right away, but in big stores or malls you should ask staff for the fitting room. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

english: Do you have this in size M?
vietnamese: Cái này có size M hông?
pronunciation: kai nay co size em hong?
example_sentence: Cái giày này có size 38 hông chị?
example_translation: Do you have this shoe in size 38?
notes: The English word "size" is commonly used; sellers will usually reply "we have it" or "sold out." In the South people often add an informal question tag meaning "right?", so this is casual shop language.

example_sentence: Cái áo này có màu khác hông? Em muốn màu xanh.
example_translation: Does this shirt come in other colors? I want the blue one.
notes: Use this casual Southern phrasing to ask if there are other color options; it's informal and commonly used in everyday, market or shop conversations.

english: Is it on sale? / Is there a promotion?
vietnamese: Hàng có giảm giá hay khuyến mãi hông?
pronunciation: hang co guam gia hay khuyen mai hong?
example_sentence: Hôm nay hàng có giảm giá hay khuyến mãi hông?
example_translation: Is there a sale or promotion today?
notes: Use the formal term "promotion" for stores and supermarkets. At local markets—especially in the South—sellers usually use a casual phrase meaning "cut the price" when bargaining.

example_sentence: Cái này tính bằng thẻ được hông?
example_translation: Can I pay for this by card?
notes: Many small shops only accept cash, so if they say no, accept it and have cash ready. This is a casual Southern expression, suitable for markets and street vendors but not for formal situations.

example_sentence: Cửa hàng nhỏ này chỉ nhận tiền mặt nha.
example_translation: This small shop only accepts cash.
notes: A common notice at markets and small shops — you’ll see or be told this if you try to pay by card. It’s everyday, informal usage.

example_sentence: Cho em hóa đơn với, em trả bằng thẻ.
example_translation: Please give me the receipt, I'm paying by card.
notes: Ask for a receipt when you need proof for a warranty or a tax refund; regular street markets usually don't issue invoices.

english: No need to give change / Keep the change
example_sentence: Cứ để em, hông cần thối lại đâu.
example_translation: Keep it, no need to give me change.
notes: Use it casually to tell a vendor they can keep the change as a tip or to avoid needing small coins. "Hông" is the Southern dialect form of "không."

example_sentence: Em mua rồi mà không vừa, có đổi trả được hông?
example_translation: If I buy and it doesn't fit, can I return/exchange it?
notes: Use this casual Southern phrasing to ask whether a shop accepts returns or exchanges; big stores often have return policies, while market stalls usually don’t. It's informal—use a more polite/formal wording with staff you don't know or in official stores.

example_sentence: Cái màu này hết hàng rồi, chỉ còn màu khác thôi.
example_translation: This color is out of stock, only other colors remain.
notes: Commonly used by sellers to indicate an item is out of stock; they may offer to order it for you or suggest an alternative. Neutral, widely used in markets, shops, and informal settings across southern Vietnam.

example_sentence: Cái đó bên kho còn hàng nha.
example_translation: That item is still in stock at the warehouse.
notes: Opposite of "out of stock" — in markets "in stock" can mean either available immediately or available but you’ll need to wait while they fetch it from the back/warehouse. It’s a common, casual phrase used in everyday shopping.

vietnamese: Gói quà giúp em được hông?
pronunciation: goy kwa zoop em duoc hong?
example_sentence: Chi ơi, gói quà giúp em được hông? Em mua tặng bạn.
example_translation: Hey, can you wrap this as a gift for me? I'm buying it for a friend.
notes: Casual Southern phrasing to ask shop staff to gift-wrap (the "hông" marks Southern speech and "giúp em" is informal). Many small stores will wrap for free; supermarkets usually offer wrapping but may charge a fee. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Em muốn thử cái áo này, phòng thử đồ ở đâu vậy?
example_translation: I want to try this shirt on, where is the fitting room?
notes: Use this at clothing stores to ask where the fitting room is; staff will usually point it out or escort you in. Neutral, everyday phrasing commonly used in the South.

example_sentence: Giá này tính thuế rồi hông anh?
example_translation: Is this price inclusive of tax?
notes: Most retail prices already include VAT, but double-check for big purchases or imported items. "Hông" is a Southern, informal form of "không," so use it with shopkeepers or friends, not in formal situations.

example_sentence: Cái điện thoại này mua có bảo hành hông?
example_translation: Does this phone come with a warranty?
notes: Ask about a warranty and keep the receipt for electronics or expensive purchases—official stores usually give a warranty card. The word "hông" is a Southern, casual pronunciation; use "không" in formal situations.

english: Can you hold it for me?
vietnamese: Giữ giúp em cái này được hông?
pronunciation: zu zoop em kai nay duoc hong?
example_sentence: Em chạy ra gửi đồ nhanh, giữ giúp em cái này được hông?
example_translation: I'll quickly go drop something off, can you hold this for me?
notes: Use this casual Southern phrase to ask a shop worker or vendor to hold your order while you step away — "được hông?" and "em" make it informal and typically used by younger speakers. In small markets vendors often keep items free for familiar customers, but bigger stores may require a deposit or refuse. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Hôm nay có khuyến mãi gì hông?
pronunciation: hom nay co khuyen mai zee hong?
example_sentence: Em vô xem chút, hôm nay có khuyến mãi gì hông?
example_translation: I'm looking around, is there any promotion today?
notes: Use this to ask about current discounts or promotions—"khuyến mãi" is commonly seen on signs and ads in supermarkets and big stores. The example uses the Southern casual "hông" for "không," so it's informal speech.

english: Do you have a smaller/bigger size?
vietnamese: Có cái nhỏ hơn/ lớn hơn hông?
pronunciation: co kai nho hon / lon hon hong?
example_sentence: Cái áo này hơi rộng, có cái nhỏ hơn hông?
example_translation: This shirt is a bit big, do you have a smaller one?
notes: Use when something doesn’t fit and you want a different size — saying “smaller” or “bigger” is a simple, casual way to ask. The question-ending word is a Southern colloquial marker, so it’s fine with vendors or friends but swap to the standard/polite phrasing in formal settings.

english: Can you show me another one? / Show me the other one
vietnamese: Cho em coi cái khác được hông?
pronunciation: cho em coy kai khak duoc hong?
example_sentence: Em không ưng cái này lắm, cho em coi cái khác được hông?
example_translation: I'm not sure about this one, can you show me another?
notes: Use this casual Southern phrasing to ask shop staff to show more options—employees will often bring extra samples to compare. It's informal and typical of a younger speaker; use a more neutral or polite phrasing if you need to be formal. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Anh ơi, gọi xe giúp em với, em đang đứng trước cửa tiệm.
example_translation: Hey, call a ride for me, I'm standing in front of the shop.
notes: Use this when asking someone to call a ride for you — a polite but casual request suitable for friends, staff, or drivers. In Southern speech people often add a vocative and use a friendly "help me" phrasing that includes the word for "younger person" to sound politely familiar. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Đặt Grab xe máy / Grab xe hơi
pronunciation: daht Grahp seh mah-ee / Grahp seh hoy
example_sentence: Em đặt Grab xe máy đi nhanh hơn, chứ đường tắc dữ lắm.
example_translation: I'll book a GrabBike to go faster, the traffic is really bad.
notes: Southerners often shorten this to "book Grab" in casual speech; add "GrabBike" (motorbike) or "GrabCar" (car) to specify the vehicle.

example_sentence: Tài xế nói mấy phút nữa, nhưng em hỏi: 'Bao lâu tới?'
example_translation: The driver said a few minutes, but I asked: 'How long until arrival?','notes':'Dùng khi muốn biết thời gian chờ. Miền Nam nói nhanh: "Bao lâu tới?"
notes: A casual Southern way to ask how long until something or someone arrives (e.g., a bus or friend); Southerners often say it quickly and drop extra words.

example_sentence: Anh ơi, từ đây tới chợ giá bao nhiêu hông?
example_translation: Hey, from here to the market how much is it?
notes: Use this to ask the fare for a trip or ride; in Southern speech people often add a casual tag (pronounced like "hong") to turn it into a question. It's informal—fine for taxis or motorbike taxis but avoid in very formal situations.

example_sentence: Em nói: 'Tới chợ Bến Thành nha', tài xế trả lời: 'Dạ, tới chợ Bến Thành.'
example_translation: I said: 'To Ben Thanh Market please,' the driver answered: 'Yes, to Ben Thanh Market.'
notes: Use to ask or confirm someone's destination; this short, casual expression is common in Southern Vietnam.

example_sentence: Em chờ ở cổng lớn, anh tài xế thấy là chạy vô nha.
example_translation: I'll wait at the main gate, the driver will see and come in.
notes: Use this casual phrase to ask a driver where to pick you up when they report their location; "em" is an informal/polite self-reference. In Southern speech, "chờ" is pronounced softly. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Tới rồi, lên xe đi cho lẹ, chứ mưa chắc ướt bây giờ.
example_translation: We're here, get on the vehicle quickly, otherwise you'll get wet in the rain.
notes: Short, common phrase to invite someone into a vehicle; in Southern speech, "đi" often adds a sense of urging or impatience.

example_sentence: Anh tài xế ơi, cho em xuống đây thôi, gần tới rồi.
example_translation: Driver, let me get off here, we're almost there.
notes: Use this to ask the driver to stop so you can get off; it’s common in Southern speech. This phrasing is polite and slightly humble, especially when addressing a male driver. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Dừng ngang đây được hông, để em mua ly cà phê nhanh?
example_translation: Can you stop here so I can quickly buy a coffee?
notes: A common Southern Vietnamese, informal way to ask "is that OK?" instead of the standard form. Use it for casual permission requests (e.g., "Can you stop here?") with friends or family.

example_sentence: Quẹo trái ở ngã tư đó nha, tài xế, chậm lại một chút.
example_translation: Turn left at that intersection, driver, slow down a bit.
notes: Use the Southern colloquial verb for "turn" rather than the standard term; it's casual and commonly used when giving directions to drivers (e.g., "turn left/right").

example_sentence: Đi thẳng tới đèn đỏ rồi quẹo phải nhé.
example_translation: Go straight to the traffic light then turn right.
notes: A short, common phrase used when giving directions (walking or driving); Southern speakers use it very naturally in casual speech.

example_sentence: Em lên xe ôm, hỏi: 'Anh có mũ bảo hiểm hông?'
example_translation: I got on the motorbike taxi and asked: 'Do you have a helmet?','notes':'Luật bắt buộc đội mũ bảo hiểm trên xe máy; tài xế GrabBike thường có mũ phụ cho khách.
notes: Casual Southern phrase used when getting on a motorbike taxi or asking a driver if there’s a helmet; Vietnamese law requires helmets, and GrabBike drivers often have an extra one for passengers.
