english: How many people can it carry?
example_sentence: Chiếc xe này chở được mấy người hông? Em có hành lý nữa.
example_translation: How many people can this vehicle carry? I also have luggage.
notes: Casual Southern way to ask how many people a vehicle can carry—commonly used for small cars or motorbike taxis. Informal, so choose a more formal wording in polite or official situations.

example_sentence: Chở hành lý chút xíu được hông, em có một vali nhỏ.
example_translation: Can you carry some luggage? I have a small suitcase.
notes: Ask beforehand to make sure the driver can carry your luggage or if you should request a larger car; this is casual Southern Vietnamese (hông = không).

example_sentence: Tối nay tắc đường dữ hông, em sợ muộn bữa tiệc.
example_translation: Is the traffic really bad tonight? I'm afraid I'll be late for the party.
notes: “Dữ” is a Southern Vietnamese intensifier meaning “very,” used in casual speech. Use it when asking how bad something is or to estimate time—e.g., to judge how long traffic will delay you.

example_sentence: Anh ơi đổi địa chỉ được hông, em muốn ghé thêm chỗ mua đồ.
example_translation: Can I change the address? I want to stop by another place to shop.
notes: Usually tell the driver beforehand; Grab’s app has a route-change option but it may charge a fee.

example_sentence: Sao kẹt rồi, em hủy đặt xe đi nha, để đặt lại sau.
example_translation: Traffic is stuck, I'll cancel the booking and rebook later.
notes: On ride‑hailing apps like Grab, repeatedly canceling bookings can incur penalties; use the phrase meaning "cancel the ride" when you want to cancel a trip.

vietnamese: Thanh toán bằng thẻ hay tiền mặt?
pronunciation: tahn twan bahng thay hi tee-en maht
example_sentence: Tài xế hỏi: 'Anh trả thẻ hay tiền mặt?', em trả lời: 'Tiền mặt.'
example_translation: The driver asked: 'Card or cash?', I answered: 'Cash.'
notes: Use this when asking how to pay—ride apps like Grab accept cards and e-wallets, but cash is still commonly used in the South. It's a casual, everyday question.

example_sentence: Em trả tiền mặt nha, anh có tiền thối hông?
example_translation: I'll pay cash, do you have change?
notes: Use this casual phrase when you want to pay in cash—common with drivers or street vendors; in the South it's informal. Ask first whether they have change. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

english: Give me the driver's phone number
vietnamese: Cho em số điện thoại tài xế
pronunciation: chaw em saw dee-en thwahy tie seh
example_sentence: Cho em số điện thoại tài xế để em gọi khi tới cổng nha.
example_translation: Give me the driver's phone number so I can call when I'm at the gate.
notes: Use this to ask for the driver’s phone number when you need to contact them directly. Grab often shows the number in the app, but you may still have to ask someone to share it. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Em đặt xe đi tới sân bay Tân Sơn Nhất, sáng mai 5 giờ xuất phát.
example_translation: I booked a ride to the airport, leaving at 5 AM tomorrow.
notes: Use when telling someone to go to the airport. Advise arranging transport early to avoid missing the flight and to check for any extra airport fees.

example_sentence: Gần tới hông? Em sợ tài xế đi vòng lâu quá.
example_translation: Are we almost there? I'm worried the driver is taking a long route.
notes: Use this casual way to ask if you're almost at your destination; "hông" is the Southern colloquial for "không," so it's common in everyday speech with friends, family, or drivers but not in formal settings.

example_sentence: Em trả tờ 200k, anh có tiền thối hông?
example_translation: I pay with a 200k note, do you have change?
notes: Common in the South — drivers often don’t have small change, so this casual phrase is useful and you should try to have exact change to avoid hassle.

example_sentence: Ở chợ có mấy chú xe ôm truyền thống luôn đứng chờ khách.
example_translation: At the market there are several traditional motorbike taxi drivers waiting for customers.
notes: Refers to the traditional, street‑hired motorbike taxi (not app‑booked like GrabBike); very common in Southern Vietnam and used in casual, everyday speech.

vietnamese: Đi cẩn thận nha / Chú ý an toàn
pronunciation: dee kun thahn nha / choo ee an tawn
example_sentence: Lên xe thì nhớ nói: 'Anh ơi đi cẩn thận nha, em vội mà sợ tắc.'
example_translation: When getting on the vehicle say: 'Please drive carefully, I'm in a hurry and worried about traffic.'
notes: Use this to remind a driver to slow down and stay safe; in Southern speech it’s said politely, addressing the driver as "older brother" or "older sister" and adding a soft friendly ending particle. | chú = younger uncle / man your parents' age

example_sentence: Anh ơi, phòng này cho thuê hông?
example_translation: Hey, is this room for rent?
notes: Use when asking if a room or house is available for rent. In the South people often add "ơi" as a friendly call and say "hông" instead of "không," so this is casual/informal.

example_sentence: Em thích sống ở chung cư hơn nhà trọ vì an ninh tốt hơn.
example_translation: I prefer living in an apartment building to a boarding house because security is better.
notes: Means an apartment building with many separate units; commonly used in big cities—young people in Saigon often rent small “mini” apartments for convenience. Neutral, everyday usage.

example_sentence: Em đang tìm phòng trọ gần chỗ làm, rẻ chút là được.
example_translation: I'm looking for a boarding room near work, something cheap is fine.
notes: A common, informal term for a small, low-cost private room rented individually; used in everyday conversation and housing ads. In Southern Vietnam people favor this term over the more formal expression "room for rent."

example_sentence: Chủ nhà dặn đóng tiền thuê trước ngày mồng 5, tụi mình nhớ nha.
example_translation: The landlord told us to pay rent before the 5th, remember that.
notes: Use "chủ nhà" for the owner of a house or apartment and "chủ trọ" for someone who rents out multiple rooms; in the South people often speak casually and address landlords directly if they're familiar.

example_sentence: Người thuê trước dọn ra rồi, phòng trống liền.
example_translation: The previous tenant moved out already; the room's empty now.
notes: Refers to the person who pays the rent. In Southern Vietnam people commonly use the equivalent of "tenant" (often shortened) in classifieds or casual questions, and "boarder" is used for someone lodging.

example_sentence: Chủ nhà nói phải đặt cọc một tháng tiền thuê.
example_translation: The landlord said you have to put down a one-month deposit.
notes: In Vietnam landlords typically require a deposit of 1–2 months' rent—make sure the contract states the exact amount and the conditions for refund. In the South people commonly refer to it simply as "cọc."

example_sentence: Nhớ đọc kỹ hợp đồng thuê coi có mục phạt gì hông nha.
example_translation: Remember to read the lease carefully to see if there are any penalties.
notes: Always get a signed, written lease—people in the South commonly insist on a clear contract with unfamiliar landlords to avoid disputes.

vietnamese: Thuê theo tháng / Tiền thuê hàng tháng
pronunciation: thway tay thahng / tee-en thway hahng thahng
example_sentence: Tiền thuê hàng tháng bao nhiêu? Em tính trả một tháng một lần.
example_translation: How much is the monthly rent? I plan to pay once a month.
notes: Landlords usually expect monthly payments; when negotiating (a common, casual practice in the South) you can offer to pay 3–6 months up front to get a lower rate.

example_sentence: Giá thuê bao nhiêu một tháng? Có giảm cho sinh viên hông?
example_translation: How much is the rent per month? Is there a discount for students?
notes: Use this to ask directly about the rent. In the South people often haggle and ask about discounts or concessions (e.g., student rates or shared-housing arrangements).

example_sentence: Tiền điện nước và mạng tính riêng hay bao vô tiền thuê?
example_translation: Are electricity, water and internet billed separately or included in the rent?
notes: Ask whether utilities are included in rent or split between tenants to avoid misunderstandings. In the South people often use a shortened, casual term to mean utilities (often including internet).

example_sentence: Tháng này tiền điện cao quá, chắc do máy lạnh chạy nhiều.
example_translation: This month's electricity bill is too high; probably because the AC ran a lot.
notes: In cities the electricity bill is usually metered; in rented rooms it’s often split evenly among tenants. In Southern Vietnamese people commonly shorten “electricity bill” to just “electricity.”

example_sentence: Tiền nước tháng này có bao nhiêu, chủ nhà báo giúp em với.
example_translation: How much is the water bill this month? Please let me know.
notes: Water charges can be metered or a flat rate; in shared housing people usually split it evenly—ask how it’s calculated from the start.

example_sentence: Mạng nhà tệ quá, em kêu chủ hỗ trợ sửa mạng liền nha.
example_translation: The internet here is terrible; I'll ask the landlord to fix it right away.
notes: Internet is a key factor when renting, especially for work or study. In Southern Vietnam people casually describe unreliable service as a "spotty" or "weak" connection.

example_sentence: Phòng có đầy đủ nội thất, chỉ xách đồ vô ở thôi.
example_translation: The room is fully furnished; just bring your stuff and move in.
notes: Means the place comes with basic furniture—bed, wardrobe, kitchen fittings, etc. In the South this is commonly used in casual rental ads and often written informally as "full furniture" or "furniture available."

vietnamese: Không có nội thất / Hông có nội thất
example_sentence: Phòng hông có nội thất, nếu thuê phải mua đồ thêm nha.
example_translation: The room doesn't have furniture; if you rent it you'll need to buy stuff.
notes: In Southern Vietnamese this phrase often appears in a more casual, colloquial pronunciation in everyday speech; for official matters like rental contracts use the standard wording, since agreements usually specify the furniture condition at handover.

example_sentence: Dự kiến em dọn vào cuối tháng này, chủ nhaokê hông?
example_translation: I plan to move in at the end of this month; is that okay, landlord?
notes: Use when stating the official start date of the lease. In the South, tenants often casually negotiate the move-in date with the landlord.

example_sentence: Em báo trước 30 ngày trước khi dọn ra nha chủ, để trả tiền cọc cho đúng.
example_translation: I'll give 30 days' notice before moving out so the deposit can be handled properly.
notes: When you vacate, make a written handover/inspection report to avoid disputes over the security deposit. In Southern Vietnamese, speakers often use a formal term for handing the room back to the landlord and a more casual phrase for simply moving out, so match your wording to the situation.

example_sentence: Tủ lạnh hư, em nhắn chủ nhà tới sửa chữa giùm nha.
example_translation: The fridge is broken; I'll message the landlord to have it repaired, okay?
notes: Report broken items to the landlord so they can arrange repairs. In the South people commonly use short, casual urgent phrases equivalent to "fix it now" or "please fix" when they need something done immediately.

example_sentence: Em tới xem phòng 6 giờ chiều được hông?
example_translation: Can I come view the room at 6 PM?
notes: Viewing the room is an important step before deciding; landlords usually set a specific appointment, and in the South people use short, casual questions when arranging it.

example_sentence: Anh có thể giữ phòng giúp em 1 ngày để em sắp xếp giấy tờ hông?
example_translation: Can you hold the room for me for one day so I can arrange the paperwork?
notes: Reserving a room usually requires a small deposit—without it the owner may give the room to someone else. In the South people often say "giữ dùm" as a more casual way to ask someone to hold it.

vietnamese: Chấm dứt hợp đồng trước hạn
pronunciation: chahm zut hop dong trook hahn
example_sentence: Muốn chấm dứt hợp đồng trước hạn thì phải báo trước 30 ngày và có thể mất tiền cọc.
example_translation: If you want to break the lease early you must give 30 days' notice and you might lose the deposit.
notes: Contracts usually state required notice, penalties, or deposit deductions for early termination. In the South, tenants commonly ask directly about the penalty amount when they plan to leave early.

example_sentence: Hợp đồng sắp hết, anh muốn gia hạn thêm 6 tháng được hông?
example_translation: The contract is about to end; would you like to renew for another 6 months?
notes: Renewing a lease usually involves negotiating a new rent; in southern Vietnam people often ask the landlord directly in person as the contract is about to expire.

example_sentence: Giá thuê này có bao điện nước hông? Nếu bao thì tiện lắm.
example_translation: Does this rent include electricity and water? If so it's very convenient.
notes: Rental ads will state whether electricity and water are included; in the South people commonly ask casually “included or not?” to find the total cost, so use this informal phrase when checking ads or asking landlords.

example_sentence: Em muốn ở ghép để tiết kiệm, có ai cần tìm bạn cùng phòng hông?
example_translation: I want to share a place to save money; does anyone need a roommate?
notes: Informal phrase commonly used by students and young professionals when seeking shared housing. In the South people often post in Facebook groups or place ads saying "Looking for roommates." | bạn = friend/peer (neutral, same age)

example_sentence: Khi dọn ra, chủ nhà có hoàn tiền cọc đầy đủ hông?
example_translation: When I move out, will the landlord refund the full deposit?
notes: Deposits are often reduced for damage or unpaid bills, so photograph the item at handover as evidence. In Southern speech people commonly use a casual way to ask “Will you refund the full deposit?” — use this informal phrase to confirm the refund in person.

example_sentence: Chỗ bến xe ở đâu hông?
example_translation: Where is the bus station?
notes: Used to ask where something or somewhere is; in Southern speech people often add a short final question particle to make it more casual. Replace the generic "place" with the specific location (e.g., the hospital).

example_sentence: Làm sao để tới chợ Bến Thành dạ?
example_translation: How do I get to Ben Thanh Market?
notes: Use when asking for directions; add a polite word or particle when speaking to elders or strangers. In the South people often use a more colloquial word order that literally means “how to go to…”.

example_sentence: Đi thẳng tới ngã tư rồi rẽ phải nha.
example_translation: Go straight to the intersection then turn right.
notes: Very commonly used when giving directions—especially for main roads—and you can add a distance after it (e.g., "100 m").

example_sentence: Tới đèn thì rẽ trái, quẹo vô hẻm thứ hai.
example_translation: At the light turn left, then go into the second alley.
notes: Southern speakers commonly use a colloquial form meaning "turn into" when directing someone into an alley or narrow side street; it's informal and used in everyday directions. Use it for turning into a small lane/side street rather than for a general "turn left" command.

example_sentence: Rẽ phải đi thẳng khoảng 200m là tới nha.
example_translation: Turn right and go straight about 200m and you'll arrive.
notes: Use "turn into" before naming an alley or street; adding a soft final particle (common in Southern Vietnamese) makes the direction sound more casual and friendly.

example_sentence: Cửa hàng ở ngã tư đó, nhìn thấy cây xăng là đúng chỗ.
example_translation: The shop is at that intersection; you'll see a gas station.
notes: Refers to a four-way intersection. In the South people often give directions by naming landmarks at the intersection (e.g., “the intersection with the gas station” or “the lighted intersection”); it's casual, everyday usage.

example_sentence: Ngã ba kia rẽ trái vô hẽm nhỏ nha.
example_translation: At that T-junction, turn left into the small lane.
notes: Refers to a three-way (T) junction and is often used when giving directions in alleys. Common in Southern (Mekong Delta) speech and used in casual, everyday directions to indicate the exact turning spot.

example_sentence: Qua đường chỗ đèn xanh rồi đi tiếp nha.
example_translation: Cross at the traffic light then continue walking.
notes: "Qua đường" is the common phrase; "băng qua" stresses the action of crossing (often quickly or across traffic). In Saigon, be careful when crossing streets because there are many motorbikes.

example_sentence: Nhà em ở trong hẻm, rẽ vô hẻm thứ hai bên phải.
example_translation: My house is in the alley; turn into the second alley on the right.
notes: Alleys are key to addresses in Southern Vietnam (especially Saigon), with locations often given by hẻm. In casual Southern speech people say "vô hẻm" (vô instead of the standard vào) to mean "go into the alley."

example_sentence: Ra đường lớn rồi quẹo trái sẽ thấy trường học.
example_translation: Go out to the main road then turn left and you'll see the school.
notes: Use to mean a main, easily identifiable road (versus a small street or alley); neutral and commonly used in Southern Vietnamese when giving directions.

example_sentence: Chỗ đó có xa hông?
example_translation: Is that place far?
notes: Used to ask whether something is far; in Southern speech people often use a relaxed, informal pronunciation of the negation word, so the question sounds casual rather than formal.

example_sentence: Có quán cà phê gần đây hông?
example_translation: Is there a coffee shop nearby?
notes: Common in everyday, casual speech. Add the Southern question particle "hông" at the end to make a yes/no question.

example_sentence: Bệnh viện ở phía sau chợ, đi thẳng rồi rẽ phải là tới.
example_translation: The hospital is behind the market; go straight then turn right to get there.
notes: Use "phía sau" to say something is located behind another object or place—name a clear reference point so the listener can picture it. It's neutral and commonly used in Southern Vietnamese.

example_sentence: Công ty ở trước nhà thờ, ngay góc đường đó.
example_translation: The company is in front of the church, right at that corner.
notes: Use to say something is located in front of a place. In Southern speech it's commonly used casually with local landmarks (street corner, tree, utility pole) as reference points.

example_sentence: Tiệm nước bên cạnh hiệu sách, chị thấy hông?
example_translation: The drink stall is next to the bookstore; do you see it?
notes: Use to say two things are directly beside each other; it’s interchangeable with other words meaning “next to” and is very common in everyday, neutral/casual speech.

example_sentence: Quán ăn ở bên kia đường, đối diện trạm xe buýt.
example_translation: The restaurant is across the street, opposite the bus stop.
notes: Use "bên kia" (e.g., "bên kia đường") in casual speech; "đối diện" is a bit more formal but also commonly used.

english: Take the first street on the left
vietnamese: Rẽ vô đường thứ nhất bên trái
pronunciation: zeh voh doo-ong thuut nuht ben chai
example_sentence: Tới ngã tư thì rẽ vô đường thứ nhất bên trái nha.
example_translation: At the intersection turn into the first street on the left.
notes: In Southern Vietnamese, speakers often use a colloquial short form of "into" when giving directions — casual and common in street instructions. Use the word meaning "first" (or simply say "the first street") to mean "take the first street on the left."

english: How long will it take to get there?
vietnamese: Mất bao lâu để tới đó?
pronunciation: mut bao low day tuh dow
example_sentence: Mất bao lâu để tới sân bay dạ?
example_translation: How long will it take to get to the airport?
notes: Use this to ask how long a trip will take; add "dạ" to sound polite. Southern speakers commonly answer in minutes or hours.

example_sentence: Đi bộ được hông? Có xa hông?
example_translation: Is it far? Can I walk there?
notes: Use "hông" in casual Southern Vietnamese; speakers often ask about distance together with the mode of travel (walking, motorbike, etc.).

english: Turn around / Go back the other way
example_sentence: Trời, đi nhầm đường rồi, quay lại đi nha.
example_translation: Oh, we took the wrong way; turn back, please.
notes: Use when you want someone to head back the way they came or return to the starting point. This is neutral, everyday language commonly used in Southern Vietnamese.

example_sentence: Anh dừng ở đây giùm em được hông?
example_translation: Can you stop here for me, please?
notes: Southern speakers often add a colloquial particle to requests to ask someone to do something for them—it's more casual than the standard word for "help." Use the verb for "stop" when asking a driver to halt a vehicle (car, motorbike, or taxi), as in telling a taxi to stop here.

example_sentence: Quay về đường cũ đi, em để quên đồ ở nhà đó.
example_translation: Go back to the old road; I forgot something at home.
notes: Emphasizes returning to your starting point—use when you realize you’re lost or want to change direction. Neutral, everyday phrasing commonly used in Southern speech.

english: Follow this road / Continue along this street
example_sentence: Đi theo đường này tầm 500m là thấy bưu điện bên tay phải.
example_translation: Follow this road about 500m and you'll see the post office on the right.
notes: Use this to give simple directions (e.g., "follow this road" or "go this way"), typically followed by a distance or a landmark. It's common, everyday language in the South and neutral in register.

example_sentence: Tiệm ở góc đường, ngay quẹo trái là thấy liền.
example_translation: The shop is at the corner; turn left and you'll see it right away.
notes: Use "góc" to indicate a landmark-like position (e.g., street corner or corner of a house); Southern speakers especially favor it for clear, visual directions.

english: Traffic light / Red light / Green light
vietnamese: Đèn giao thông / Đèn đỏ / Đèn xanh
pronunciation: den yao thong / den daw / den sin
example_sentence: Qua đèn đỏ phải chờ, khi đèn xanh mới được chạy qua nha.
example_translation: You must wait at the red light; only go when the light turns green.
notes: When giving directions, mention traffic lights—stop on red and go on green; in the South people often casually remind others to "cross at the light" in crowded areas as a safety tip.

example_sentence: Mấy người ơi! Giúp em với, em té gãy tay!
example_translation: Hey everyone! Help me, I fell and broke my arm!
notes: Use to call for immediate help; in the South, speakers often use a "help me" phrasing that signals youth or familiarity, or shout a colloquial "you folks" to attract passersby — both are informal and urgent. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Gọi xe cấp cứu đi, người kia bị chảy máu nhiều!
example_translation: Call an ambulance, that person is bleeding a lot!
notes: The emergency number in Vietnam is 115; response is faster in cities and may be slower in remote areas, so give a precise address or clear nearby landmarks.

example_sentence: Gọi công an lẹ đi, tụi nó chạy mất rồi!
example_translation: Call the police quickly, they ran away!
notes: The emergency police number is 113; in southern Vietnam people commonly use the informal local word for police in everyday calls instead of the more formal term.

example_sentence: Cháy nhà kìa! Gọi cứu hỏa với!
example_translation: The house is on fire! Call the fire brigade!
notes: Shout a short, loud warning and immediately call the fire brigade at 114. This is an urgent, informal exclamation—people in markets or neighborhoods often rush together to try to douse flames before firefighters arrive.

example_sentence: Em bị thương nặng ở chân, giúp em với!
example_translation: I'm badly injured in the leg, help me!
notes: Use the first-person form used by younger speakers or when you want to sound humble; it's informal. To say where you're hurt, add "on/in [body part]" after the phrase (e.g., "on my arm"). | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Em sắp ngất rồi, cho em ngồi xuống với!
example_translation: I'm about to faint, please let me sit down!
notes: Use "sắp" to say something is about to happen (e.g., "I'm about to faint"); it's casual. If someone faints, people commonly raise their legs and call for medical help. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Em bị nghẹn, ai biết sơ cứu chỉ em với!
example_translation: I'm choking, can someone who knows first aid show me!
notes: Use this in an emergency when food or an object is blocking your airway; say it loudly and clearly so bystanders know to perform the Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts). It's a neutral, urgent phrase—appropriate everywhere in Southern Vietnam, no formal wording needed. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Cầm máu đi, đừng để nhiều máu chảy!
example_translation: Stop the bleeding, don't let so much blood flow!
notes: An urgent first-aid command: press a clean cloth firmly on the wound to stop bleeding and call emergency services if it won’t stop. It's standard Vietnamese (not dialect-specific) and used in direct, emergency situations.

example_sentence: Em gãy xương chân, đừng di chuyển em nữa!
example_translation: I broke my leg, don't move me anymore!
notes: If you suspect a broken bone, immobilize the area (use a splint) and avoid moving it. In the South people commonly say "broken bone" and will use "broken arm" or "broken leg" to specify the location.

example_sentence: Ông ấy kêu đau ngực rồi, hình như bị đau tim!
example_translation: He's complaining of chest pain, it seems like a heart attack!
notes: This is a common term. If someone has chest pain, shortness of breath, or heavy sweating, call Vietnam’s emergency number 115 immediately and have them sit down and loosen tight clothing.

example_sentence: Em vừa ăn hải sản, bị dị ứng ngứa khắp người!
example_translation: I just ate seafood and I'm allergic with itchiness all over!
notes: Clearly tell your helper what you’re allergic to; severe reactions (swollen face, trouble breathing) need immediate emergency care. In Southern Vietnam, "dị ứng" is the everyday word for allergy.

example_sentence: Uống nước lạ xong em bị ngộ độc, đau bụng và nôn ói kịch liệt.
example_translation: After drinking strange water I was poisoned, severe stomach pain and vomiting.
notes: Use when reporting food poisoning to a doctor, pharmacist, or family—say your symptoms, when they began, and which food or drink you suspect. In Vietnam people commonly use the term "food poisoning" to mean illness caused by contaminated food.

vietnamese: Rò rỉ ga / Có mùi ga
pronunciation: roh ree gah / kaw moo-ee gah
example_sentence: Có mùi ga trong bếp, rò rỉ ga kìa, ai biết tắt van không?
example_translation: There's a gas smell in the kitchen, a gas leak — can someone shut the valve?
notes: The word "ga" is the common Vietnamese term for gas; if you smell gas, turn off the stove, open windows to ventilate, avoid lighting any flames, and call a technician or emergency services.

example_sentence: Đừng chạm vào, người đó vừa bị điện giật!
example_translation: Don't touch, that person just got an electric shock!
notes: Use in an electric-shock emergency: don’t touch someone still in contact with live electricity—turn off the power or use an insulating object to separate them, then call emergency services. Practical, neutral phrasing with no special Southern-dialect features.

example_sentence: Người đó đang co giật, để em đỡ cái đầu, gọi xe cấp cứu liền!
example_translation: That person is having a seizure, I'll support their head, call an ambulance now!
notes: Use this urgent instruction when someone is having a seizure: don’t put anything in their mouth—turn them onto their side to keep the airway clear and call 115 (Vietnam emergency medical services) immediately.

example_sentence: Có người bị đuối nước ở đó, cứu với!
example_translation: Someone is drowning over there, help!
notes: In the South there are many rivers and canals; when someone is drowning, reach them with a life ring or long pole rather than jumping in unless you’re a strong swimmer. Call local rescue services if the situation is serious.

example_sentence: Bệnh viện ở mô? Em cần cấp cứu gấp!
example_translation: Where's the hospital? I need urgent care!
notes: In Southern Vietnamese, "mô" is the casual equivalent of "where" used in informal speech. When calling for help, give the nearest hospital name or a precise address/landmark (shop, gas station) so responders can find you.

example_sentence: Em cần bác sĩ gấp, đau dữ quá!
example_translation: I need a doctor urgently, the pain is severe!
notes: Add "urgent" (gấp) to show it's an emergency; public hospitals often have long waits. For life‑threatening cases, call 115 for an ambulance. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly) | bác = older aunt or uncle / older adult

vietnamese: Số khẩn cấp: 115 (xe cứu thương), 113 (công an), 114 (cứu hỏa)
pronunciation: suh kun kehp: mot mot lam (seh koo thuong), mot mot ba (kong an), mot mot bon (koo hwah)
example_sentence: Ghi nhớ số khẩn cấp: 115, 113, 114, để ai cần là gọi liền.
example_translation: Remember emergency numbers: 115, 113, 114 so anyone in need can call immediately.
notes: 115 = ambulance, 113 = police, 114 = fire; many areas also have local hotlines. Use these only for real emergencies—speak calmly and clearly give your exact address when calling.

vietnamese: Đừng cử động / Cứ nằm yên
pronunciation: doong koo doong / kuh nahm yen
example_sentence: Em gãy xương rồi, đừng cử động, cứ nằm yên đợi cấp cứu!
example_translation: I broke a bone, don't move, stay still and wait for help!
notes: Use when you suspect a spinal injury or broken bone. "Cứ nằm yên" is a gentle, calming way to tell someone to stay still if they're panicking.

example_sentence: Em thở hông được, sắp ngộp rồi!
example_translation: I can't breathe, I'm about to suffocate!
notes: Use "hông" instead of "không" to show a Southern (informal) accent. If someone truly can't breathe, call 115 (Vietnam emergency ambulance) immediately and help them sit upright to ease breathing. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Con em bị lạc ở chợ, ai thấy bé chỉ em với!
example_translation: My child is lost at the market, if anyone sees them point them out to me!
notes: Use this expression to report that someone (often a child) is lost; it’s a neutral, urgent way to ask for help. In crowded places like markets people commonly announce it over a loudspeaker or ask nearby security/police to assist the search. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Em bị cướp, lấy mất ví và điện thoại, giúp em gọi công an!
example_translation: I've been robbed, they took my wallet and phone, help me call the police!
notes: Use this when reporting you've been robbed—try to remember the robber's features, the getaway vehicle and direction to tell the police. In Southern Vietnam, "cướp" is the common word for "rob." | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Em bị móc túi trên xe buýt, mất thẻ và ví rồi!
example_translation: I got pickpocketed on the bus, lost my cards and wallet!
notes: Use this casual Southern expression to say you were pickpocketed—it's common in crowded places and on public transport. If you lose cards or documents, quickly block your bank cards and report the theft to the police. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Việc này khẩn cấp, em cần xe cấp cứu ngay!
example_translation: This is urgent, I need an ambulance right away!
notes: Use to emphasize urgency when calling for help or when speaking with medical staff or the police. It’s a neutral, appropriate phrase for formal situations with emergency responders and to indicate a serious, pressing problem.

example_sentence: Chào em, lâu ghê hông?
example_translation: Hi, long time no see, right?
notes: Use informally with friends or a romantic partner. In the South people often add "em"/"anh" by age or status, and "hông" is the Southern form of "không."

vietnamese: Dạo này em sao rồi hông?
pronunciation: zow nay em sow roy hong
example_sentence: Dạo này em sao rồi hông, công việc có ổn không?
example_translation: How have you been lately, is work okay?
notes: A casual, friendly (often flirty) text opener meaning "How have you been lately?" — "hông" is Southern colloquial for "không," so use it only in informal messages. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Tối nay rảnh hông, đi chơi hông?
example_translation: Are you free tonight, want to hang out?
notes: Short, direct, and very common—especially in Southern speech—for casually inviting acquaintances to hang out; add a simple "are you free?" to politely ask when they're available.

english: Want to go on a date?
vietnamese: Muốn hẹn hò với anh hông?
pronunciation: moo-uhn hen haw voy ahn hong
example_sentence: Muốn hẹn hò với anh hông, cuối tuần này?
example_translation: Want to go on a date with me this weekend?
notes: “Hẹn hò” means “date.” Use “anh” or “em” depending on your role with the other person; “hông” is Southern colloquial for “không” and makes the question softer and informal. | anh = older male (use for men older than you or similar age)

example_sentence: Sáng mai đi uống cà phê hông, quán kia dễ thương lắm.
example_translation: Wanna grab coffee tomorrow morning? That place is cute.
notes: Very common for a first-date invite; "coffee" is a safe, low‑pressure choice. This phrasing is Southern and informal.

example_sentence: Trưa nay em rảnh hông, đi ăn cùng anh đi.
example_translation: Are you free this noon, want to eat with me?
notes: Used to invite someone to eat — very casual, friendly Southern usage; "cùng" emphasizes doing it together.

example_sentence: Anh thích em, thiệt đó, chứ không đùa đâu.
example_translation: I like you, for real, I'm not joking.
notes: This verb expresses a lighter, less serious feeling than "to love" and is used in casual contexts. In Southern speech people often add a small particle meaning "really" to emphasize sincerity. | anh = older male (use for men older than you or similar age) | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Anh yêu em nhiều lắm, đừng lo nha.
example_translation: I love you a lot, don't worry.
notes: An intimate line for when you’re already close (anh is a male speaker addressing em, often a younger or female partner). In Southern speech you can add "nha" or "nè" to make it sound softer and more casual. | anh = older male (use for men older than you or similar age) | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Nhớ em quá, tối qua ngủ hông được.
example_translation: I miss you so much, I couldn't sleep last night.
notes: Simple and very common — a casual, intimate way to say "I miss you," often followed by words meaning "so" or "very" for emphasis. In Southern speech negatives are pronounced differently and a colloquial form is used for "can't." | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Hồi nhỏ em có crush thầm lâu lắm rồi.
example_translation: I had a crush secretly for a long time when I was young.
notes: Younger speakers commonly use the English loanword "crush" informally; use the native Vietnamese equivalent meaning "someone you secretly like" for a more polite or formal tone. | mình = I/me (casual, friendly — used between close friends)

example_sentence: Em dẫn bồ về giới thiệu tụi bạn nha.
example_translation: Bring your boyfriend/girlfriend to meet my friends, okay?
notes: Use "boyfriend"/"girlfriend" in polite or formal contexts; the informal slang for a romantic partner is very common in Southern speech and sounds slightly intimate. Avoid the slang in formal situations or when speaking with elders. | bạn = friend/peer (neutral, same age)

example_sentence: Cho anh hôn đi, lần này thôi nha.
example_translation: Let me kiss you, just this once, okay?
notes: Kissing is often private in Vietnam, so ask for consent beforehand. Even in the more relaxed South, respect personal boundaries and get permission.

example_sentence: Để anh ôm em một chút cho ấm.
example_translation: Let me hug you for a bit to make you feel warm.
notes: An intimate, casual gesture used between romantic partners or close friends and often used to comfort someone. Not appropriate with acquaintances or in formal situations.

example_sentence: Đi bộ đi, nắm tay anh đi nha.
example_translation: Let's walk, hold my hand, okay?
notes: Used to show a public, intimate relationship; in the South it's a casual, romantic gesture commonly seen among young couples.

example_sentence: Em dễ thương quá, anh nhìn hoài không chán.
example_translation: You're so cute, I could look at you forever.
notes: A common casual compliment meaning "cute"; Southern speakers often add an intensifier to make it stronger (like saying "so cute"). Use it with friends, family, or romantic interests—avoid in formal situations or with strangers. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Đừng ghen nha, anh chỉ quen biết thôi mà.
example_translation: Don't be jealous, I'm just acquaintances with them.
notes: Used to express jealousy; in conversation it’s often followed by reassuring or calming phrases to ease tension and is common in casual speech.

example_sentence: Mình chia tay đi, anh thấy không hợp nữa rồi.
example_translation: Let's break up, I feel we don't fit anymore.
notes: A common phrase for ending a relationship; it can sound gentle or firm depending on the context.

english: Let's be official / Be my boyfriend/girlfriend
example_sentence: Mấy tháng rồi thân quá rồi, làm người yêu nhau nha?
example_translation: We've been close for months, let's be official, okay?
notes: The wording "be my boyfriend/girlfriend" is the more formal way to ask; ending the question with a friendly final particle (very common in Southern speech) softens it and makes it sound more casual and approachable.

vietnamese: Cho em số điện thoại đi
pronunciation: cho em saw dee-en thoy dee
example_sentence: Gặp vui quá, cho em số điện thoại đi nhé.
example_translation: This was fun, give me your phone number, okay?
notes: A very common, casual way to ask to keep in touch; in Southern speech "số điện thoại" is often shortened to "số" or the slang "số phone." | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Tới nơi nhớ nhắn tin cho em nha.
example_translation: Text me when you arrive, okay?
notes: Use this verb for SMS or chat messages. Adding casual sentence-final particles makes it sound friendlier and informal—these are very common in Southern Vietnamese. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Rảnh thì gọi em đi, em muốn nghe giọng anh.
example_translation: Call me when you're free, I want to hear your voice.
notes: Use to ask someone—usually a family member or close friend—to call you instead of texting. It's casual Southern usage; "em" suggests the speaker is younger or lower in status, so avoid in formal situations. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

vietnamese: Dẫn em đi gặp bạn bè nha
pronunciation: yun em dee gap bahn bay nha
example_sentence: Tuần tới dẫn em đi gặp bạn bè coi cho vui.
example_translation: Next week take me to meet your friends so it's fun.
notes: Asking to be taken to meet someone's friends often signals making the relationship public to their social circle. It's casual—common in Southern speech with a friendly softening particle—and typically used in dating to show commitment or become “official.” | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly) | bạn = friend/peer (neutral, same age)

vietnamese: Dẫn về ra mắt ba mẹ
pronunciation: yun vay ra mut bah meh
example_sentence: Nếu ổn thì dẫn em về ra mắt ba mẹ nha.
example_translation: If it's okay, take me home to meet your parents, okay?
notes: Use this when formally introducing a partner to their parents — in Vietnam it's regarded as a major, committed step, so treat it respectfully and seriously.

example_sentence: Cuối tuần đi coi phim hông, có bộ mới đó.
example_translation: Wanna go see a movie this weekend? There's a new one.
notes: In Southern Vietnamese, "coi" replaces "xem"; suggesting a movie is a casual, low‑pressure, and commonly accepted first‑date idea.

example_sentence: Xin chào, anh ơi!
example_translation: Hello, brother!
notes: A polite, general greeting used in Southern Vietnam; in casual speech locals often shorten it to just "hello" or say hello plus a familiar title (e.g., ma'am or miss).

example_sentence: Chào, lâu quá hông gặp!
example_translation: Hey, long time no see!
notes: Casual, friendly greeting used among friends or acquaintances, often followed by a pronoun or name (e.g., "hi + name"). Common in Southern Vietnamese and informal, so avoid in formal situations.

example_sentence: Em khỏe hông? Công việc ổn hông?
example_translation: How are you? Is work ok?
notes: A Southern casual way to ask "How are you?" used with friends, family, and peers. Add the appropriate familiar pronoun depending on your relationship—use the form for someone younger, an older man, or an older woman. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Dạ, em hiểu rồi.
example_translation: Yes, I understand.
notes: Polite way to say “yes,” used with older people or customers and more respectful than the casual affirmative.

example_sentence: Hông sao đâu, đừng lo.
example_translation: No problem, don't worry.
notes: Southern colloquial form of "no," widely used in casual conversation; sounds friendly and informal. Avoid it in formal speech or writing.

example_sentence: Cảm ơn chị nhiều nha.
example_translation: Thank you very much, sis.
notes: A standard polite thank you; Southern speakers often add a friendly particle or the listener’s pronoun afterward to sound warmer (e.g., “Thank you, sir” or “Thank you, ma’am”).

example_sentence: Hông có chi, lần sau cần nói liền ha.
example_translation: No problem, let me know next time.
notes: A very common Southern, casual reply to “thank you” (more informal than “không có gì”), used among friends or in relaxed situations.

example_sentence: Xin lỗi nha, em vô trễ xíu.
example_translation: Sorry, I came in a bit late.
notes: Used for apologies or to get attention. Southerners add “nha” to soften the apology.

example_sentence: Em hông hiểu anh nói gì, anh nói lại được hông?
example_translation: I don't understand what you said, can you say it again?
notes: Choose em/anh/chị to match your relationship (age/status); "hông" is Southern colloquial for "not," so this is informal, spoken Vietnamese. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Làm ơn cho em xem thực đơn với.
example_translation: Please let me see the menu.
notes: Polite when asking for something; in very casual situations you can omit it and just use a short "give me..." style request instead.

example_sentence: Cái này bao nhiêu tiền vậy, chị?
example_translation: How much is this, ma'am?
notes: Use this to ask the price when shopping; in Southern Vietnam people often shorten it into a very casual, clipped question in busy markets. It's informal—fine with street vendors but avoid in formal situations.

example_sentence: Toilet ở đâu vậy? Em cần xíu.
example_translation: Where's the toilet? I need it a bit.
notes: The English loanword "toilet" is widely used and fine for everyday situations; in more formal places use the polite Vietnamese term for restroom, and Southerners often pronounce the loanword like "tee-let."

example_sentence: Em đói quá, mình ăn đi ha.
example_translation: I'm so hungry, let's eat.
notes: Use em/anh/chị to match your relation to the listener (younger speaker: em; older male: anh; older female: chị). Quá is a Southern, informal intensifier meaning "very," making the phrase sound natural and casual. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Em khát nước, cho em ly nước đá với.
example_translation: I'm thirsty, give me a glass of ice water please.
notes: A common, casual expression — adding the word for “water” clarifies you mean wanting a drink (not a metaphorical longing). Widely used in Southern speech; use the informal first‑person pronoun when you’re younger or speaking with friends/family. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Đi thôi, kẹt xe tới nơi rồi.
example_translation: Let's go, traffic will get worse soon.
notes: A casual, informal way to invite someone to leave or move on—use with friends or family. In Southern speech people often repeat the verb (e.g., "go, go") to urge someone more strongly.

example_sentence: Chờ xíu nha, em lấy ví khóa liền.
example_translation: Wait a moment, I'll grab my wallet quickly.

example_sentence: Giúp em với, máy hư không chạy được.
example_translation: Help me, the machine's broken and won't run.
notes: Use this short, casual Southern request to ask for immediate help—the extra "with" element makes it sound urgent; add a softening ending to make it less abrupt. example_sentence: Anh đi đâu vậy? Em đi theo luôn nha.
example_translation: Where are you going? I'll come along.
notes: Casual question. In the Southern dialect it’s common in speech and texting to use a very colloquial pronunciation/spelling instead of the standard form.

example_sentence: Em tên gì, cho anh biết đi?
example_translation: What's your name? Tell me, please.
notes: Choose the kinship pronoun based on relative age and gender—if you’re younger, address an older man or woman accordingly; if you’re older, use the form for a younger person. example_sentence: Em tên là Lin, hổng biết anh tên chi?
example_translation: My name is Lin, what's your name?
notes: Use a pronoun that reflects your role/age (younger person, older brother, older sister); in Southern speech people often add a casual follow-up question, so this is informal and friendly. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

pronunciation: chaw em mot lee kah feh, yah
example_sentence: Cho em một ly cà phê sữa đá, dạ.
example_translation: Give me an iced milk coffee, please.
notes: In the South, "Cho em..." is the usual, friendly way to request something (e.g., ordering food/drinks); "em" is a first‑person pronoun used by younger speakers and is gender‑neutral.
