example_sentence: Em thích cái này lắm, mua liền đi.
example_translation: I really like this, buy it now.
notes: Casual way to say you like something—add a colloquial "very" to emphasize. Use the appropriate first-person pronoun (Southern speech favors informal pronouns) and keep the tone informal. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Hông sao, em tự lo được mà.
example_translation: No problem, I can handle it myself.
notes: A very common, casual reassurance meaning “no worries” or “it's okay.” It's a Southern, more colloquial form than the standard phrase and used informally among friends.

example_sentence: Sao rứa, sao mặt mày buồn quá?
example_translation: What's up, why do you look so sad?
notes: A Southern colloquial word meaning “so/that,” used in casual, regional speech among friends (e.g., “What’s up?”); it sounds very local and should be avoided in formal or unfamiliar situations.

example_sentence: Tốt rồi, gặp lại sau nha!
example_translation: All good, see you later!
notes: Casual farewell used with friends and peers; in the south people often add a friendly sentence‑final particle to sound warmer. For formal situations use a more polite expression that literally means “see you again.”

example_sentence: Em hông muốn đi đâu hết.
example_translation: I don't want to go anywhere.
notes: Casual Southern Vietnamese for "no/not," commonly used with friends and family; avoid in formal writing or polite situations with strangers.

example_sentence: Dạ, em biết rồi cô ơi.
example_translation: Yes, I know already (ma'am).
notes: In Southern Vietnamese, "dạ" is commonly used as a polite, attentive "yes"—use it with elders or in service situations; among close friends you’ll more often hear "ừ" or "uh."

example_sentence: Ủa, anh ở đây hả? Sao không báo em biết?
example_translation: Huh, you're here? Why didn't you tell me?
notes: Very common interjection in the South for surprise or mild confusion. Informal; tone depends on context (questioning, shocked, etc.).

example_sentence: Tối nay đi ăn hông? Chỗ mới ngon lắm.
example_translation: Wanna go eat tonight? There's a new place that's delicious.
notes: A simple, everyday invitation—Southern speech uses the colloquial question particle "hông" instead of "không". Very casual; use only with friends, family, or coworkers you know well.

example_sentence: Hẹn 7 giờ nha, hen?
example_translation: See you at 7, okay?
notes: A Southern, informal short form of "hẹn" used to confirm plans—equivalent to "see you"/"deal"; in writing use the standard "hẹn" or the full phrase.

english: Can you handle it? / You down?
example_sentence: Làm tiếp bữa nay chịu hông?
example_translation: Do you want to continue working tonight — can you handle it?
notes: Means "Can you handle it?" or "You down?". It's a very colloquial Southern form (hông = không), used among friends to ask if someone agrees, can endure, or is willing—often playful or challenging—so avoid it in formal or polite situations.

example_sentence: Con nhỏ hát ghê hông? Mấy người mê luôn!
example_translation: That girl sang amazingly, right? People loved it!
notes: Use "ghê" to show either fear or strong admiration—tone and expression decide which. "Ghê hông?" is a casual Southern tag question meaning roughly "scary, huh?" or "wow, right?"

example_sentence: Ăn xong, nằm nghỉ sướng quá trời.
example_translation: After eating, lying down feels so good.
notes: Used to say something feels great, physically or emotionally; common in casual Southern speech and often intensified with words meaning "so" or "too" (e.g., "so good").

example_sentence: Bữa đó party hết sẩy luôn, quẩy tới sáng!
example_translation: That party was awesome, we partied until morning!
notes: Slang to emphasize something is extremely good. Very colloquial and typically Southern; not for formal contexts.

example_sentence: Em có bồ hông?
example_translation: Do you have a boyfriend/girlfriend?
notes: Casual, commonly used in Southern speech to mean boyfriend/girlfriend or romantic partner; use terms like "boyfriend/girlfriend" or "romantic partner" in very formal contexts.

example_sentence: Con xe mới của anh xịn dữ luôn.
example_translation: His new car is really fancy.
notes: Used to praise something as fancy, classy, or authentic. Widely used across Vietnam but often in casual speech in the South.

english: To lie / to exaggerate / to be cocky
example_sentence: Đừng xạo nữa, ai tin mấy chuyện đó đâu.
example_translation: Stop lying/exaggerating, nobody believes that stuff.
notes: Southern slang meaning to lie or brag; used informally among friends to tease ("you're exaggerating") or scold ("don't be cocky") and not appropriate for formal situations.

example_sentence: Hôm nay đi làm thấy lìu xìu muốn ngủ.
example_translation: Today at work I feel so sluggish I want to sleep.
notes: Describes being tired, listless or weak. Very colloquial and affectionate-sounding; common in the South.

example_sentence: Đừng có chảnh, ai cũng mệt khi ở gần mấy người vậy.
example_translation: Don't be snobby; everyone gets tired around people like that.
notes: Used to call someone arrogant or acting superior. Informal and often used among young people to criticize attitude.

example_sentence: Mình đổi kế hoạch rồi, ổn hông?
example_translation: I changed the plan, is that ok?
notes: A very common, casual Southern way to ask "Is it okay?" The key word is a shortened form meaning "okay"/"all right"; use it among friends or in informal settings, not in formal speech.

example_sentence: Em dỗi rồi đó, anh vô làm lành đi.
example_translation: I'm sulking, go make up with me.
notes: Casual: used for light, playful sulking—often romantic or childlike. In Southern Vietnam it’s commonly used jokingly between couples.

example_sentence: Hết hồn luôn, tưởng mất đồ rồi.
example_translation: I was so startled — I thought I lost my stuff.
notes: Common expression for being shocked or startled. Can be used humorously or seriously depending on context.

example_sentence: Đừng có nói tầm bậy trước mặt người lớn.
example_translation: Don't talk nonsense in front of the elders.
notes: Used to call out nonsense in casual Southern speech. Informal and can sound rude, so avoid with elders or in formal situations.

example_sentence: Giỡn đó mà, đừng giận hoài!
example_translation: Just kidding, don't stay mad!
notes: A casual Southern way to say "just kidding"—use giỡn đó with friends and family; giỡn hoài means "joking all the time" and is informal, so avoid it in formal or polite settings.

english: To grind / hustle (work or game hard)
example_sentence: Mấy bữa nay em cày game tới khuya luôn.
example_translation: These days I grind/play games until late at night.
notes: Originally 'plow', now slang for working or playing intensely (studying, gaming, working). Widely used among youth.

example_sentence: Đừng đú theo mấy trend vô bổ đó.
example_translation: Don't try to show off by following those useless trends.
notes: Very trendy slang meaning to fake it or show off. Popular among youths on social media; negative connotation sometimes.

example_sentence: Đừng có nói lời bậy bạ trước mặt tụi nhỏ.
example_translation: Don't say inappropriate things in front of the kids.
notes: Used to call something inappropriate, silly or indecent. Informal and commonly used by parents and elders, too.

english: Come on / stop it (soften a request)
example_sentence: Thôi mà, em xin lỗi rồi mà, đừng giận nữa.
example_translation: Come on, I already apologized, don't be mad anymore.
notes: Softens an appeal or request; extremely common in Southern conversational speech. Adds warmth or pleading tone.

example_sentence: Món này ngon quá trời luôn, ăn hoài không chán.
example_translation: This dish is so delicious, I could eat it forever.
notes: Southern flavor intensifier meaning 'very' or 'extremely'. Often used in casual praise or exaggeration.

example_sentence: Cuối tuần rảnh hông? Đi cafe đi.
example_translation: Are you free this weekend? Let's go for coffee.
notes: Casual way to ask a friend if they're free. "Hông" is the Southern pronunciation of "không" — use with peers, not in formal or respectful situations.

example_sentence: Anh ăn cơm hông?
example_translation: Are you going to eat rice?
notes: "Cơm" means cooked rice or a main meal; in the South people say "ăn cơm" to mean eating the main meal (not snacking). It's neutral, everyday language.

example_sentence: Chị ăn đi, còn nóng lắm.
example_translation: Eat, it's still very hot.
notes: Basic verb meaning "to eat"; used in casual invitations (e.g., "come eat") and combined directly with dish names (e.g., "eat noodle soup," "eat cake"). It's standard across dialects and informal when used as an invitation.

example_sentence: Món này ngon quá trời!
example_translation: This dish is extremely delicious!
notes: Used to praise food; in Southern speech people often emphasize it with slang like "quá trời" or "ngon dữ" — casual/informal.

example_sentence: Em đói quá, đi ăn đi.
example_translation: I'm so hungry, let's go eat.
notes: Use this word to say you're hungry. In the South people often add an emphatic "so" ("so hungry") and use it casually to suggest going to eat right away.

example_sentence: Em ăn xong rồi, no bụng rồi.
example_translation: I've finished eating, I'm full.
notes: Use the casual word for "full" in everyday speech; add the word meaning "stomach" to make clear you mean full from eating.

example_sentence: Sáng mình ăn phở gà hông?
example_translation: Shall we have chicken phở this morning?
notes: A famous Vietnamese soup — in the South you'll find both beef and chicken versions, and people commonly add fresh herbs to taste; it's a casual, everyday dish.

example_sentence: Nay ăn bún nha?
example_translation: Shall we have bún today?
notes: This word refers broadly to rice vermicelli noodle dishes (e.g., crab-based, fermented-fish, or beef versions); in Southern Vietnam there are many local variants, so specify the type when ordering. It's an everyday, casual term used at markets and street stalls.

example_sentence: Hủ tiếu Mỹ Tho ngon lắm, em thích ăn ở đó.
example_translation: My Tho hủ tiếu is very tasty; I like eating there.
notes: Popular in Southern Vietnam, especially the Mekong Delta around Mỹ Tho; it’s served either dry (no broth) or with broth. It’s casual, everyday/street food rather than formal cuisine.

example_sentence: Sáng em hay ăn bánh mì thịt.
example_translation: In the morning I often eat a bánh mì with meat.
notes: A common street food—especially in the South, vendors sell bánh mì all day with many fillings like meats, chả, pâté, and egg. Use this casual, everyday term when ordering or talking about the sandwich.

example_sentence: Cho em hai cuốn gỏi cuốn nha, ít nước mắm.
example_translation: Give me two gỏi cuốn, please with less fish sauce.
notes: Eaten fresh (not fried) and usually dipped in mixed fish sauce or peanut sauce; this is the Southern term for the fresh spring roll.

example_sentence: Chả giò giòn lắm, ăn lúc nóng là nhất.
example_translation: The fried rolls are crispy; they're best eaten hot.
notes: In the South this dish is called "chả giò" (in the North it's usually "nem rán"), so use chả giò when speaking Southern Vietnamese. It's typically served with fresh herbs and nước chấm (fish‑sauce dipping sauce).

example_sentence: Nước mắm ở đây mặn vừa, em thích lắm.
example_translation: The fish sauce here has the right saltiness; I like it a lot.
notes: A staple seasoning in Vietnamese cooking—Southerners typically mix fish sauce with sugar, lime (or vinegar), chili, and garlic into a sweet‑savory dipping sauce used at everyday meals.

example_sentence: Chấm bánh xèo vô nước mắm nha.
example_translation: Dip the bánh xèo into the fish sauce, okay?
notes: Means to dip a bite of food into sauce; used very commonly when eating wrapped dishes (like fresh rolls) and fried items. Casual, everyday usage.

example_sentence: Mẹ nấu canh chua ngon lắm, ăn với cơm là tuyệt.
example_translation: Mom's sour soup is very tasty; eating it with rice is great.
notes: Canh refers to a light soup (e.g., vegetable, sour, or crab soup) eaten with rice as part of a meal — unlike phở, which is a standalone main-course noodle soup.

example_sentence: Hải sản ở Vũng Tàu tươi lắm.
example_translation: Seafood in Vũng Tàu is very fresh.
notes: In Southern Vietnam—especially along the coast—seafood is typically very fresh and is bought at markets or eaten at specialty restaurants. Use this term when talking about local specialties or ordering food casually; it's everyday, not formal, vocabulary.

example_sentence: Tôm chiên này to quá, ăn đã ghê.
example_translation: These fried shrimp are huge, really satisfying to eat.
notes: Use "tôm" to mean shrimp in everyday speech—it's common in Southern Vietnamese and appears in many dishes (fried, grilled, stir‑fried, hotpot, etc.).

example_sentence: Cá kho ăn với cơm nóng ngon dễ sợ.
example_translation: Braised fish with hot rice is amazingly delicious.
notes: This is the general word for any fish or fish dish—use it for fried, steamed, grilled, or braised preparations. In Southern Vietnam people commonly eat caramelized clay‑pot fish with rice; the term is neutral and used in everyday speech.

example_sentence: Sáng em mua trái cây về, có xoài với dừa.
example_translation: This morning I bought fruit home; there are mangoes and coconuts.
notes: Southern Vietnam is abundant in tropical fruits (mango, jackfruit, coconut, durian), and people there commonly eat fruit daily. Use this as casual cultural context when talking about food habits or regional specialties.

example_sentence: Xoài chín ngọt, ăn với muối ớt ngon lắm.
example_translation: Ripe mango is sweet; eating it with chili salt is very tasty.
notes: In Southern Vietnam, raw mango is commonly eaten as a casual street snack with chili-salt, shrimp salt, or a strong fermented fish sauce. There are many local mango varieties.

example_sentence: Sầu riêng thơm nhưng hông phải ai cũng ăn được.
example_translation: Durian smells strong but not everyone can eat it.
notes: Use when talking about the fruit or travel warnings — durian is widely grown in southern Vietnam but often banned from buses and hotels because of its strong smell.

example_sentence: Cái bánh này bao nhiêu tiền?
example_translation: How much is this pastry?
notes: Use this standard, neutral question when buying snacks or food at markets. You can sometimes haggle in open-air markets, but restaurants and eateries usually have fixed prices.

example_sentence: Cho em tính tiền nha, dạ.
example_translation: Please give me the bill, thanks.
notes: Use this to ask for the bill at a restaurant or cafe; in Southern Vietnam people often use a younger-sounding self-pronoun to sound polite and casual, while a neutral/formal pronoun is better in more formal or upscale settings.

example_sentence: Cho em một phần cơm sườn với canh chua nha.
example_translation: Give me one portion of rice with ribs and sour soup, please.
notes: Use this polite, casual phrase to order a portion—use the form that a younger speaker would use and add a friendly sentence-ending particle to sound warmer. It's common in Southern Vietnam at street stalls and casual eateries; older customers typically use a more formal first-person form. | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Cho em một ly trà sữa ít đường nha.
example_translation: Please give me a milk tea with less sugar.
notes: Use this when ordering drinks to ask for less, no, or half sugar—customers commonly specify the sugar level. In Southern Vietnam people often use a casual "reduce sugar" phrasing, so it's informal and fine for cafes or street vendors.

example_sentence: Quán hủ tiếu hết rồi, mình ăn phở hông?
example_translation: The hủ tiếu shop is sold out; shall we have phở instead?
notes: Use it to tell customers a dish or stall is sold out; it's casual and commonly heard at small eateries or market stalls in the Southern dialect when food runs out quickly.

example_sentence: Em đi làm bằng xe máy mỗi ngày.
example_translation: I go to work by motorbike every day.
notes: Use this term as the everyday, neutral word for motorcycle in Southern Vietnam — people commonly use it to refer to personal motorbikes for daily transport.

example_sentence: Xe ga chạy êm, em thích đi xe ga hơn.
example_translation: Scooters run smoothly; I prefer riding an automatic scooter.
notes: Xe ga refers to automatic scooters (no gear shifting). Very popular in the city for ease of use.

example_sentence: Xe số mạnh, đi đường trường ổn hơn.
example_translation: Manual bikes are powerful and better for long rides.
notes: Use this to mean a manual-gear motorbike (as opposed to an automatic scooter) when renting, buying, or asking about transport; it's a common, neutral term in Southern speech.

example_sentence: Đội mũ bảo hiểm vô nha, dạ em đội rồi.
example_translation: Put on your helmet, yes I'm wearing it already.
notes: Helmets are legally required, so use the phrase for "put on a helmet" when reminding someone to wear one. In Southern speech people commonly say đội mũ and often use vô instead of the more formal vào.

example_sentence: Anh đội mũ cho chắc đi chứ hông được để lỏng.
example_translation: Put your helmet on properly, you shouldn't leave it loose.
notes: Use this informal verb to tell someone to put on their helmet—Southern speakers commonly say it as a friendly reminder before heading out.

example_sentence: Giao thông bữa nay kẹt quá, đi chậm luôn.
example_translation: Traffic is jammed today, everything's moving slowly.
notes: Refers to traffic in general. In Southern Vietnamese, people commonly say "kẹt" (casual) to mean traffic is jammed.

example_sentence: Hổng đi đường Nguyễn Huệ giờ, kẹt xe dữ lắm.
example_translation: Don't go on Nguyễn Huệ now; the traffic jam is terrible.
notes: This is the everyday word for a traffic jam; in Southern speech people often add a casual intensifier meaning “very” to emphasize it, so it's commonly used in informal conversation.

example_sentence: Đừng bấm còi hoài nghe, làm ồn người ta á.
example_translation: Don't keep honking; it makes noise for others.
notes: It means to press the horn; honking is common on busy streets, but excessive or rude honking is frowned upon.

example_sentence: Đừng vượt ẩu trên đường trường, nguy hiểm lắm.
example_translation: Don't overtake recklessly on the highway; it's very dangerous.
notes: Use this verb to mean to overtake or pass (vehicles) or figuratively to surpass someone. In Southern speech, locals commonly warn against "reckless overtaking" — a casual everyday warning among drivers.

example_sentence: Đậu xe chỗ này hông được, dễ bị phạt nha.
example_translation: You can't park here; you'll likely get fined.
notes: Both đậu xe and đỗ xe mean “to park” (commonly used for motorbikes) and are interchangeable. In cities, be careful—parking rules can be strict in some areas, so watch signs and payment/attendant rules.

example_sentence: Gởi xe ở bãi giữ xe gần đó cho an tâm.
example_translation: Leave the bike at the nearby parking lot to be safe.
notes: A paid parking area for motorbikes and bicycles where an attendant usually watches the vehicles for a small fee. It's a common, informal service throughout southern Vietnam.

example_sentence: Dừng ở cây xăng này đổ xăng cho đầy.
example_translation: Stop at this gas station and fill up the tank.
notes: This is the common Southern Vietnamese word for gas stations; people typically say "fill up" (i.e., get gas) there in casual speech.

example_sentence: Đổ xăng đầy đi cho khỏi lo giữa đường.
example_translation: Fill up the tank so you won't worry about running out on the road.
notes: A common, casual Southern phrase meaning "fill up with petrol"; most stations take cash, and in cities some also accept cards or mobile payment apps.

example_sentence: Anh quên bằng lái ở nhà, hông biết sao giờ.
example_translation: I forgot my driver's license at home; I don't know what to do now.
notes: Common, neutral term for a driver's license (often shortened from "driver's license") — widely used in the South. Always carry it when driving, as traffic police commonly ask to see it during stops.

example_sentence: Chở 3 là dễ bị phạt lắm, đừng có liều.
example_translation: Carrying three people easily gets you fined; don't risk it.
notes: Use this expression to say someone receives a fine or punishment—commonly for traffic violations like running a red light or carrying too many passengers. It's neutral and widely used in spoken Southern Vietnamese; in formal contexts people may use a phrase meaning "to be sanctioned" or explicitly mention a monetary fine.

example_sentence: CSGT đứng chốt ở ngã tư đó, chạy chậm lại nha.
example_translation: Traffic police are stationed at that intersection; slow down.
notes: Use "traffic police" (often called CSGT) — officers commonly stop drivers to check papers and enforce rules, sometimes at random, so keep your documents handy and be polite.

example_sentence: Bật xi nhan trước khi rẽ chứ hông?
example_translation: Turn on your signal before you turn, okay?
notes: Xi nhan is the common term for indicators/turn signals. Using it is polite and safer; many riders forget to use it.

example_sentence: Phanh gấp dễ té lắm, giữ khoảng cách cho chắc.
example_translation: Sudden braking can make you fall; keep a safe distance.
notes: Phanh means "to brake" — use it when slowing or stopping a vehicle; in Southern Vietnamese people often warn "té" ("fall") instead of the northern "ngã."

example_sentence: Nếu gặp tai nạn thì kêu cứu thương liền nha.
example_translation: If there's an accident, call the ambulance right away.
notes: Use to refer to accidents — especially traffic accidents; in Vietnam dial 113 (police), 115 (ambulance), or 114 (fire) in emergencies, and locals usually memorize these numbers. Neutral register; used in both casual and formal speech.

example_sentence: Đường này hông được rộng lắm, chạy chậm thôi.
example_translation: This road isn't very wide; just go slowly.
notes: Use this as the general word for road or street. In Southern Vietnamese, speakers often say "hông" (rather than "không") in casual negative questions.

example_sentence: Đường này một chiều, hổng được đi ngược nha.
example_translation: This road is one-way; you must not go the wrong way.
notes: Seen on road signs across Vietnam and used as a formal label rather than in casual talk. Driving the wrong way is dangerous and can result in fines.

example_sentence: Đừng đậu xe lên vỉa hè, cản đường người đi bộ á.
example_translation: Don't park on the sidewalk; it blocks pedestrians.
notes: Refers to the sidewalk. In Southern Vietnam people often park motorbikes on it despite rules, and enforcement varies by ward—so expect parked bikes and step around them.

example_sentence: Dân mình hay đỗ xe lên vỉa hè, hông tốt nhưng cứ thấy hoài.
example_translation: People often park bikes on the sidewalk; it's not good but you see it all the time.
notes: Use this phrase in casual conversation to say someone parked on the sidewalk. In Vietnam it’s commonly done but often illegal and can lead to fines, with enforcement and tolerance varying by area.

example_sentence: Đừng chở 3, CSGT dễ bắt phạt lắm, chở 2 ok thôi.
example_translation: Don't carry three; traffic police will easily fine you. Carrying two is okay.
notes: These short forms are common in Southern casual speech: taking one passenger (two people total) is normal, but carrying two passengers (three people total) is risky and often illegal.

example_sentence: Cho em vô bệnh viện được hông?
example_translation: Can you take me to the hospital?
notes: Use this when you need to go to the hospital for a check-up or in an emergency; in the South people commonly use a shorter, colloquial verb for "enter" instead of the more formal phrasing. Bring your ID and health insurance card if you have one.

example_sentence: Em cần gặp bác sĩ nha.
example_translation: I need to see a doctor.
notes: Use to address the doctor examining you; for older doctors say "Doctor + name" or simply "Doctor" as a polite, respectful form. | bác = older aunt or uncle / older adult

example_sentence: Y tá ơi, giúp em chút được hông?
example_translation: Nurse, can you help me a bit?
notes: Nurses usually collect samples, take blood pressure, and give injections; in hospitals, address them politely—say “nurse” with a friendly vocative or use a polite particle rather than calling abruptly.

example_sentence: Phòng khám này khám nhanh, rẻ hơn bệnh viện lớn.
example_translation: This clinic checks quickly and is cheaper than big hospitals.
notes: Refers to outpatient clinics; private ones often stay open into the evening and handle initial consultations and basic tests, and in smaller provinces you’ll commonly find general clinics covering a range of services. The term is neutral and used in everyday speech.

example_sentence: Cho em mua mấy viên thuốc ho ở nhà thuốc được hông?
example_translation: Can I buy some cough medicine at the pharmacy?
notes: Pharmacies sell both prescription and over‑the‑counter medicines; clearly describe your symptoms so the pharmacist can advise you, and bring a written prescription if the medication requires one.

example_sentence: Trường hợp cấp cứu phải đưa đi ngay.
example_translation: In an emergency, (you) must take (them) there immediately.
notes: Use for accidents, heavy bleeding, or when someone stops breathing; it refers to emergency medical care and the hospital emergency department and is used when calling for urgent help.

example_sentence: Gọi xe cứu thương liền đi, người ta té rồi!
example_translation: Call an ambulance now, someone fell!
notes: In Vietnam dial 115 for an ambulance; expect longer waits in rural or suburban areas than in cities.

example_sentence: Em đau ở đây, đau dữ lắm.
example_translation: It hurts here, it hurts a lot.
notes: Say "it hurts in/at [body part]" to indicate location, and describe intensity with words meaning "a little," a Southern-colloquial "very/severe" intensifier, or "terrible" — the intensifier is informal/casual.

example_sentence: Em sốt mấy hôm rồi mà hông bớt.
example_translation: I've had a fever for a few days and it hasn't gone down.
notes: Used to describe having a fever; in the South people often use a casual expression meaning “I’ve had a fever for a few days.” Monitor your temperature and take fever-reducing medicine if needed.

example_sentence: Em ho hoài về đêm, ngủ hổng được.
example_translation: I keep coughing at night, I can't sleep.
notes: Tell the pharmacist or doctor whether your cough is wet (with phlegm) or dry; in Southern speech a common colloquial expression means “coughing continuously” to indicate a persistent cough.

example_sentence: Hổng biết tại sao em đau đầu suốt ngày.
example_translation: I don't know why I have a headache all day.
notes: In the South, people use the simple word for “headache” to mean an ordinary head pain; if it comes with vomiting or blurred vision, get medical help right away.

example_sentence: Em ăn xong bị đau bụng, hông biết do cái gì.
example_translation: I got a stomachache after eating, not sure why.
notes: Specify where the pain is (upper/lower, left/right) and mention accompanying symptoms like vomiting or diarrhea. This helps in medical situations and is appropriate in both casual and formal contexts.

example_sentence: Em dị ứng với hải sản, ăn vào là nổi mẩn.
example_translation: I'm allergic to seafood; I break out when I eat it.
notes: Essential when buying medicine or visiting a hospital—clearly tell the doctor or pharmacist about any drug or food allergies.

example_sentence: Bác sĩ ghi đơn thuốc rồi, em vô nhà thuốc lấy nha.
example_translation: The doctor wrote a prescription; go to the pharmacy to get it.
notes: A prescription (with the doctor’s signature) is required to buy prescription medicine. Keep it for follow-up appointments — it’s a formal medical document.

example_sentence: Thuốc này uống trước hay sau ăn hông?
example_translation: Should this medicine be taken before or after meals?
notes: Specify the medicine form (tablet, syrup, injection). In Vietnam people often ask whether it should be taken before or after meals.

example_sentence: Nhớ uống thuốc đúng giờ, đừng bỏ nha.
example_translation: Remember to take the medicine on time, don't skip it.
notes: Use "take medicine twice a day" for dosing or "finish the course" to mean complete the treatment; in Southern speech people often add a casual reminder like "don't forget."

example_sentence: Thuốc này có tác dụng phụ gì hông?
example_translation: Does this medicine have any side effects?
notes: Use this to ask a doctor or pharmacist about common side effects (e.g., nausea, dizziness) and when you should stop taking the medicine; it's a neutral, polite phrase appropriate for clinical settings.

example_sentence: Em vừa leo cầu thang là khó thở liền.
example_translation: I get short of breath right after climbing the stairs.
notes: For severe symptoms, seek emergency care; when describing shortness of breath, say whether you also have chest pain.

example_sentence: Anh ta bị té chảy máu nhiều lắm.
example_translation: He fell and is bleeding a lot.
notes: Use this in medical or emergency contexts (neutral register). If bleeding heavily, apply firm pressure and seek emergency care — be sure to distinguish nosebleeds, mouth bleeding, and external wounds.

example_sentence: Nghe tiếng rắc là biết chắc gãy xương rồi.
example_translation: If you hear a crack, you know the bone is probably broken.
notes: If you suspect a broken bone, get an X‑ray; in Southern Vietnamese people commonly use the word "gãy" for "broken" in everyday and medical contexts.

example_sentence: Bác sĩ nói huyết áp em hơi cao, phải theo dõi thường xuyên.
example_translation: The doctor said my blood pressure is a bit high; must monitor regularly.
notes: Blood pressure is routinely checked at clinics—always tell the healthcare staff if your family has a history of high blood pressure.

example_sentence: Em đã hẹn khám lúc 3 giờ chiều, nhớ dậy sớm nha.
example_translation: I have an appointment at 3 PM; remember to wake up early.
notes: For medical appointments—arrive 10–15 minutes early to complete check‑in; many clinics (especially in the South) accept bookings by phone or app.

example_sentence: Em có bảo hiểm y tế hông? Nếu có thì chi phí rẻ hơn.
example_translation: Do you have health insurance? If yes, the cost is cheaper.
notes: Use your health insurance card at public hospitals to reduce costs — present it along with your national ID (CMND) when you go for a consultation.

example_sentence: Bệnh viện gần đây ở đâu vậy?
example_translation: Where is the nearest hospital?
notes: Use this to ask for directions; in the South people commonly shorten it to just “where” plus the place name, so it’s casual and common in everyday speech.

english: I feel sick / I'm not well
vietnamese: Em thấy mệt / Em không được khỏe
pronunciation: em thay met / em khong duoc kwoe
example_sentence: Dạ, em thấy mệt lắm, hông muốn ăn gì.
example_translation: Yes, I feel very tired; I don't want to eat anything.
notes: A common, casual way to say you’re not feeling well; add the polite particle "dạ" when speaking to elders or healthcare staff. In Southern speech, speakers often use "hông" as the informal negative question word (instead of the standard "no/not"). | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)

example_sentence: Em cần làm hộ chiếu mới, hông biết phải đi chỗ nào?
example_translation: I need to get a new passport, don't know where to go.
notes: Use when applying for or renewing a passport; in Southern Vietnam people typically just use the plain word for passport in casual speech.

example_sentence: Visa em sắp hết hạn, em phải gia hạn hay rời nước luôn?
example_translation: My visa is about to expire—do I need to extend it or leave the country?
notes: In Southern Vietnam people commonly use the loanword "visa" in everyday speech instead of the more formal Vietnamese term, so use "visa" for casual conversation.

example_sentence: Dạ, cho em hỏi thủ tục xin cấp hộ chiếu như thế nào ạ?
example_translation: Excuse me, may I ask what the procedure is to apply for a passport?
notes: Use this polite phrasing when asking about documents at an office; people in the South commonly add "dạ" to show politeness.

example_sentence: Em muốn gia hạn visa, có cần hẹn trước hông?
example_translation: I want to extend my visa; do I need an appointment?
notes: Ask in advance about required documents and processing time, since many offices require an appointment or online submission.

example_sentence: Nếu lỡ ở quá hạn thì em bị phạt bao nhiêu tiền?
example_translation: If I overstay, how much fine will I get?
notes: Overstaying can lead to fines and temporary bans on re-entry; penalties and procedures vary by case. This is a formal/legal term used in official contexts.

vietnamese: Dấu nhập cảnh / dấu xuất cảnh
pronunciation: dow nyap cahn / dow soot cahn
example_sentence: Anh kiểm tra hộ chiếu coi có dấu nhập cảnh chưa hông?
example_translation: Can you check if there's an entry stamp in my passport?
notes: Immigration officers stamp your passport on arrival and departure—keep the stamp (or entry/exit card) safe to avoid problems when leaving or re-entering the country.

example_sentence: Em đang chờ thẻ tạm trú, họ nói khoảng hai tuần nữa xong.
example_translation: I'm waiting for the temporary residence card; they said it'll be ready in about two weeks.
notes: Use when speaking to foreign nationals or people with temporary residency; ask about the card’s processing time and which documents to submit with the application.

example_sentence: Công ty báo em phải có giấy phép lao động mới được ký hợp đồng dài hạn.
example_translation: The company told me I need a work permit to sign a long-term contract.
notes: Foreigners working in Vietnam must have a work permit; the process is quite complicated and employers usually handle the paperwork. This is a formal/legal term used in official contexts.

example_sentence: Dạ cho em hỏi bên công chứng ở đâu vậy? Em cần công chứng giấy tờ gấp.
example_translation: Excuse me, where is the notary office? I need to notarize documents urgently.
notes: Use "notarize" when you need documents (contracts, personal papers) officially legalized at a notary office; this is different from certification done at the local people's committee.

example_sentence: Hồ sơ bên đại sứ quán cần dịch công chứng tiếng Việt sang tiếng Anh nè.
example_translation: The embassy requires certified translation of documents from Vietnamese to English.
notes: Often required for visa or immigration paperwork. A certified translation is an officially verified translation stamped by a translation office or a notary public.

vietnamese: Đại sứ quán / Lãnh sự quán
pronunciation: die soo kwan / lan soo kwan
example_sentence: Em phải chạy lên đại sứ quán để làm lại giấy tờ, họ hẹn chiều mai.
example_translation: I need to go to the embassy to redo some documents; they scheduled me for tomorrow afternoon.
notes: Use when you need passports, visas, or assistance from your country’s authorities; embassies/consulates handle these issues—call ahead to confirm hours and required documents.

example_sentence: Cục Xuất nhập cảnh ở gần sân bay, anh đi thử hỏi coi họ chỉ chỗ nộp hồ sơ.
example_translation: The Immigration Office is near the airport; try asking them where to submit the paperwork.
notes: The main government office that handles entry/exit and visa extensions; in Ho Chi Minh City people often refer to it informally as "the immigration bureau" or simply "the bureau."

example_sentence: Em phải ra công an phường đăng ký tạm trú, dạ em đã lấy số rồi.
example_translation: I have to go to the ward police station to register temporary residence; I've already taken a number.
notes: Registering temporary or permanent residence is handled at the local ward/commune police station. Bring your residence book, lease agreement, and ID — it's an official administrative process.

example_sentence: Hết hạn căn cước rồi, em phải lên nơi cấp để làm lại.
example_translation: My citizen ID expired; I need to go to the issuing office to renew it.
notes: CCCD is the official citizen ID — foreigners often need to show an ID to prove their identity for official procedures. In the South people commonly shorten the name to "căn cước."

example_sentence: Dạ em mang sổ hộ khẩu và hợp đồng thuê nhà lên công an phường để đăng ký tạm trú.
example_translation: I brought the household registration book and rental contract to the ward police to register temporary residence.
notes: This official document is still used in many administrative procedures despite recent legal changes. When registering temporary residence you’ll often be asked to provide a copy.

example_sentence: Chị nhớ đi đăng ký tạm trú trong vòng 30 ngày sau khi tới chỗ ở mới nha.
example_translation: Remember to register temporary residence within 30 days after arriving at the new place.
notes: Formal/legal requirement: when you move to a new address you must register temporary residence; late registration may result in a warning or a fine.

example_sentence: Ở quầy cho em mấy mẫu đơn để điền xin gia hạn visa với.
example_translation: Please give me the application forms to fill out for visa extension.
notes: Different offices use their own forms—ask staff which one you need so you don’t have to make extra trips.

example_sentence: Phí làm hộ chiếu là bao nhiêu hông chị?
example_translation: How much is the passport fee, sis?
notes: Use this when paying or depositing money—always confirm the exact fee and ask for a receipt. Some services add extra charges for priority or expedited handling.

example_sentence: Em gửi hồ sơ rồi, họ nói thời gian xử lý khoảng 10 ngày làm việc.
example_translation: I submitted the documents; they said processing time is about 10 working days.
notes: Ask whether the time refers to working days or calendar days—many places count only working days.

example_sentence: Cho em hỏi có cần hẹn trước để nộp hồ sơ hông?
example_translation: Do I need to make an appointment to submit the documents?
notes: Use when arranging visits to government offices, clinics, or service centers — many require or recommend making an appointment by phone or online to avoid long waits; the phrase is neutral to slightly formal.

example_sentence: Em phải nộp giấy tờ chứng minh nơi ở và hợp đồng lao động kèm theo nha.
example_translation: You must submit supporting documents proving residence and employment contract as well.
notes: Formal administrative warning used in application forms and office notices (common in the South): always check the list of required supporting documents, because missing papers will cause your file to be returned and you’ll have to resubmit them.

example_sentence: Nếu lỡ mất hộ chiếu thì phải báo mất hộ chiếu ở đại sứ quán liền.
example_translation: If you lose your passport, you must report the lost passport at the embassy immediately.
notes: Report the loss immediately to prevent misuse — go to the police or embassy, which will arrange temporary documents or help you get a replacement passport.

example_sentence: Họ hẹn em tới để lấy dấu vân tay cho hồ sơ xin visa.
example_translation: They scheduled me to come take fingerprints for the visa application.
notes: Used for official procedures like visa or ID-card fingerprinting; be on time and wash your hands beforehand so staff can get clear prints.

example_sentence: Dạ em tới sớm, lấy số thứ tự rồi ngồi chờ tới lượt nha.
example_translation: I arrived early, took a queue number, and sat waiting for my turn.
notes: Used when taking a numbered ticket at government offices or service counters; waits can be long, so arrive early to reduce waiting. Neutral/formal — suitable for signs and polite requests.

vietnamese: Anh/Chị giúp em với được hông?
pronunciation: anh/chee zoop em voy duu-uck hong
example_sentence: Anh giúp em với được hông, em không hiểu chỗ này phải điền sao?
example_translation: Can you help me? I don't understand how to fill this part.
notes: Polite, friendly Southern way to ask for help—address someone as "anh" (older man) or "chị" (older woman) if you're younger; this phrasing is casual and regional, so avoid it in formal situations. | anh = older male (use for men older than you or similar age) | chị = older female (use for women older than you or similar age) | em = younger person (use for anyone younger than you; also how you refer to yourself humbly)
